#8288. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin said. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”

Buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the big cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they said. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

#8285. Rocks, Ridges, and Roads

I continue my trek through Pennsylvania by facing off with rocky vistas, but also smooth gravel roads.

Progress in Pennsylvania has been swift, the trail follows a relatively straight path across Kittatinny Ridge. The rocks are always a threat to slow things down, but I haven’t found it hard to do 20-25 miles a day even with daylight dwindling as the year moves forward. It feels like my last proper week on the trail. After I finish hiking on Saturday I will have just two more days remaining before heading back to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge. First things first, I need to get through this week.

Today should be somewhat eventful. I am hoping to squeeze in 25 miles, I will be crossing through a section of especially difficult rocks known as the Knife’s Edge, passing the unique Eckville Shelter, and ending near a popular viewpoint called The Pinnacle. I did well getting to sleep at a reasonable hour last night, helping me to start southbound from the Bake Oven trailhead around 7:30AM after my morning chores. My first thoughts when I got on the trail: “I am going to love hiking this last bit tomorrow!”. The trail was more of a dirt ATV path, flat, troublesome rocks removed, I could hike flat out, which I now really appreciate after the rocky sections that look flat and easy on the map but are a nuisance.

The flat trail was good while it lasted, but after a mile or so it reverted back to the typical Pennsylvania ridge hiking – a narrow, twisting path with mostly small rocks that weren’t bothersome. But then you’d look ahead and see a sea of boulders and think “the trail can’t possibly be routed through that?” And yet, that is exactly where it goes. I must not be too bothered by the rocks because I only hesitated a little when I saw a sign reading “Bear Rock” pointing to an enormous pile of rocks before sighing deeply and making my way to the top. This was no easy climb, there are blue blazes but hikers can still find plenty of ways up, none of them particularly direct.

A few more miles down the trail I came to another rocky section, but this one wasn’t optional. The trail narrowed to effectively nothing, the trail was just to follow the steeply sloped rocks and find a way to the other side. There was a decent view of the valley to the south, though more of my focus was on staying upright. This section is known as the Knife’s Edge. I don’t imagine it compares to the more famous/infamous Knife’s Edge on Katahdin. Scooby, a thru-hiker I encountered earlier in the year seemed to agree based on her comment on FarOut which I am going to shamelessly steal for your entertainment. I apologize for any language readers may find offensive:

Knife’s Edge my biffin’ boppy! The only Knife’s Edge I know is In THE GREAT NORTHERN MAINE BAXTER WILDERNESS. How dare this thin squirrely rock formation disparage the great Northern edge.

View from the AT near the Allentown Hiking Club Shelter.

I swung through the Allentown Hiking Club Shelter to retrieve a package. In a case of déjà vu, Pebbles had become separated from her Z Seat. I am told that it is actually Greasetrap to blame this time around. With the package secured, I continued along the ridge, which made up the first 14 miles of today’s hike.

The ridge continues west, but soon is divided by the Little Schuylkill River, so the Appalachian Trail shifts south to cross the river in Port Clinton. I won’t get there today, instead the trail heads south through the town of Eckville. There is a unique shelter just off the trail. The property was acquired by the National Park Service and turned into a hiker hostel/shelter in cooperation with the Blue Mountain Eagle Climbing Club, which maintains the AT in the area. In addition, Mick Charowsky, spent decades serving as the shelter caretaker. The property has a flushing toilet and a solar shower. I figured it would be worth checking out and getting a bit of water for my journey. I took a few minutes to peruse the logbook, finding a handful of familiar names, and adding my own name to the historic register.

Come with me, seat pad, you are needed up the trail!

Looking across the valley at The Pinnacle.

Looking across the valley at The Pinnacle.

The trail out of Eckville was the best so far in Pennsylvania. It was mostly a graded gravel road. I didn’t mind the gradual climb which lasted almost the entire 5 miles to The Pinnacle. By this point I had decided I would try to camp nearby so I could catch the sunset/sunrise from the overlook. I’d be coming up a few miles short of the 25 I had in mind, but I had space in my next itinerary to scoop those up. I headed straight for the rocks with my pack on and took in the scene. The Pinnacle sits at the leading edge of a ridge that drops sharply down to the valley just ahead of the viewpoint. An abundance of rocks ensure clear views. The only hitch was that the sun would be setting at the exact opposite angle from the rocks, it was the one thing you could really see. I figured it would still be perfect for sunrise tomorrow and set about finding a flat spot. I found plenty, though there were far fewer that weren’t so overcome with rocks that they seemed like they might lead to ancient Rome. I thought I had a decent spot, no rocks were visible, but when it came time to drive my tent stakes it is became clear that I had merely found a spot with about an inch of soil on top of a lifetime supply of rocks. I wiggled the stakes down until they were just about firm enough to hold for the night.

#8284. ‘He Looked Like a Moose.’ Missouri Bowhunter Rattled This 221-Inch Buck in to 10 Yards

Published Nov 12, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was cold and rainy the morning of November 6th in northwest Missouri. But the bucks were in rut chasing does, and dedicated bowhunter James Fleener was in his tree saddle long before daylight on a 320-acre hunting lease he has with his brother-in-law.

“I hunted the spot the evening before, and it was ideal,” Fleener tells Outdoor Life. “I knew there was a giant buck in the area. I had lots of trail camera photos of him. I felt good about that place. I left my saddle stand, climbing sticks and bow in the woods that night to return the next morning prepared for an all-day sit.”

Well before daylight he was in a Latitude Outdoors saddle that he used for the first time this year. For him it’s been a hunting game-changer.

“I’d hunted that deer about a dozen times, and moved slowly and quietly into the area where I figured the bucks were pushing does,” says the 26-year-old bowhunter from Lawson, Mo. “I’d hunt a spot, then move 100 yards or so to another place, and get my saddle up in another tree fast and quiet.”

The little maple tree that Fleener hunted from that November 6 morning was near a small pond with a grassy ditch feeding it. That created a natural funnel for deer, and at first light he started seeing does and small bucks.

“I cracked together my rattling antlers and pretty soon a small buck came my way,” he says. “I was watching him come to about 50 yards and I looked beyond him and I saw the big buck through my binoculars about 200 yards off.”

The buck was on the prowl, apparently looking for does. Fleener grunted loudly at the big buck, but he was far off and it was raining so the deer never heard it.

“I grabbed my rattling antlers and cracked them together as loud as I could,” says Fleener, who owns Mid-Mo Trucking Services. “When I did, his head whipped around and he came right to me at a trot. He came fast around a bean field edge. He looked like a moose coming to me at a trot.”

Fleener knew the buck was huge, and looked away for a moment to gather himself, so as not to make a mistake when the deer got in range.

“He was coming right to me and fast, so I drew my bow when he was almost 100 yards away so he wouldn’t see me move to draw,” he says. “At 10 yards he slowed down to cross the grassy ditch, and I let my arrow fly.

“He jumped but never knew what hit him. He moved away at a fast walk, got behind some cover and I thought I heard him crash, but it was wet and rainy, so I wasn’t sure.”

Fleener contacted his good friend Mason Chapman and told him he’d shot a great buck. Chapman was hunting nearby, but he immediately went to help his buddy.

About 30 minutes later Chapman met with Fleener and they tracked the buck, which ran only 40 yards before falling dead.

“When I first saw him up close I was in disbelief,” Fleener says. “This was the first year I’d hunted that lease, and although I knew he was on the property, I had no idea he was really that big.”

Read Next: How to Rattle in a Buck, Based on Whitetail Deer Research

The 14-point whitetail rough scores 221 inches, with an inside spread of about 20 inches. Its rack has a massive palmated antler, with split points on one side.

“I’m going to have a full body mount made of my buck, and I’m still in disbelief about the whole thing.

“I caught the buck in the perfect rut phase, at the right time and place.”

#8283. Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#8280. Welcome to the Outdoor Life Shop: Your New Destination for the Best Hunting, Fishing, and Camping Gear

Published Nov 12, 2026 1:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Since our very first issue published in 1898, Outdoor Life has covered outdoor gear with independence and rigor. From Jack O’Connor’s old gun columns to today’s in-depth video reviews, field testing gear and reporting the results has always been part of our publication’s DNA.

Which is why I am excited to now introduce our new online gear shop, which represents the culmination of more than a century of gear coverage. This new online retail site will carry a wide variety of quality outdoor products, and purchases made from the site will help to power the Outdoor Life you know and love into the future. There are a few key points that longtime OL readers should know.

If you’ve followed Outdoor Life closely, you know that we’re not scared to piss off folks on occasion. This often includes manufacturers who have overhyped their products. That’s because we believe that reader trust is OL’s single most important asset. If we report the truth, good or bad, we have faith that you will keep coming back. This has been the promise that the OL editors made at the very beginning, and it’s the contract we uphold today.

In all of our gear reviews and buying guides, we will continue to celebrate the top-performing products (whether they are carried in the Outdoor Life shop or not). Likewise, if a product falls short, we’ll continue to call out those flaws.

Unlike some other media outlets in our space, we have no editorial obligation to a single brand. We shoot, hunt with, and wear whatever is new and noteworthy, because that makes the most interesting content. This will continue, regardless of which brands are carried in the shop. Simply scan a few of our recent gear reviews (like our rifle scope test or binocular test) and you will find this to be true.

Over time, the shop will begin to host content from the hundreds of gear reviews we’ve written through the years. Beyond basic specs and product descriptions, the Outdoor Life shop will include details about how the products actually performed during testing. Our “editor’s picks” will highlight the top performing items in a category. Video reviews will show how products work (or don’t work) in the field.

Our aim will be to educate the reader, or potential customer, about the gear they are considering buying, whether they end up buying it from us or someone else.

The OL team is proud that we already spend a ton of time and effort producing the most in-depth gun and gear reviews in the outdoor space. We have been able to fund these efforts by linking to online retailers who sell the gear that we cover. If one of our readers purchases a product from these online retailers, we made a small commission. Added up over the course of the year, these commissions become a meaningful source of revenue that powers our editorial team to create more content.

At its best, it’s a system of meritocracy. Those who create the best content grow the biggest audiences and, in turn, make the most money — to make more content.

But that system has been corrupted with the popularization of Artificial Intelligence. Now, more and more folks are simply asking ChatGPT or Claude, “what’s the best wader for duck hunting?” These chatbots scrape online articles to produce an answer for the user, who then makes their purchase. That hunter will rarely see the original source material. In other words they will never come to our reviews and field tests at Outdoor Life.

And the chatbots don’t much care if they are lifting content from OutdoorLife.com or someone’s basement blog, or even a manufacturer’s own website. In time, this will lead to the degradation (I believe the modern term is “enshittification”) of  gear reviews, and, well, first-hand expert information in general.

Our way to combat this is to own the online shop ourselves. We believe that so long as we have the best and most thorough information, and the best available products, the reader will end up with us.

In the weeks and months to come, we will be adding many more brands and gear categories to the shop. We’ll be offering deals on select products that have performed admirably in our field testing. And we’ll be turning out a lot more stories and videos.

If you’re looking to purchase some new gear, I do hope you check out the OL shop. But the truth is, there are many reasons to love the outdoors and our passion for quality gear is only a sliver of Outdoor Life.  So, after all these years, thank you for reading, following, and watching.

#8279. Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

The Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed plan.

Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#8278. Pennine Way Wrap-Up

Although I only completed 120 miles of the Pennine Way’s 268 mile route, I learned so much.  What went wrong; what went right?  To finish up this blog, I thought I’d summarize my experiences and lessons learned for anyone else who might be considering this adventure.

Compared to the major thru-hikes in the US, the Pennine Way sees only 1,500 to 3,500 thru-hikers each year.  On the morning I started, there were only two other people leaving Edale: Owen (aka SST) and Michael.

Over the course of my journey, I crossed paths with others infrequently and briefly.  Some days, I didn’t see another person except at the pub where I had breakfast or dinner.  There is usually a village somewhere along the day’s route.  However, there are some stretches at the beginning and the end where there is nothing for two or three days.  The terrain feels vast and trackless.  If you don’t enjoy time alone, bring someone with you.

That being said, the British people were universally friendly (except the Uber drivers).  There were many times when I was saved by the kindness of strangers.

The trail is boggy and muddy in sections, rocky and treacherous in others.  Total elevation gain is more than Mount Everest.  The wind is incessant and can be powerful.  Although the temperatures stayed between a mild mid-50s to mid-60s, the wind-chill kept me bundled up even on hard climbs.

When the rain comes—and it will come—it can be anything from a light drizzle to a torrential downpour.  It might be both within the same hour.  Most of the trail provides no shelter, manmade or otherwise.  Full rain gear is essential.  A tent that can be pitched in exposed areas in rain and wind will make a big difference.

I trained for this adventure in inclement weather and on technical terrain with steep climbs.  However, the weather was worse than I had experienced and this made the terrain more challenging. Mental toughness in the face of physical hardship is a must.

I’m one of those travelers who tends to make minimal reservations and just goes where opportunity takes me.  This did not work so well for me on the Pennine.  The villages along the route are tiny and services are very limited.  You might hike all day only to find that there is no place to stay.  Campgrounds close due to weather.  Inns in the smallest villages may have less than six rooms.  Many pubs stop serving food after 6:00 pm. Shops may close by 5:00 or 5:30 pm, and don’t open again until 9:00 am.

While the notion of wild camping is romantic, it was also more challenging than I thought.  You have to be far enough away from farms and villages to remain unnoticed.  However, many of the truly remote locations are on windy, barren hilltops or boggy moors.  The mental toll of not knowing where I would end each day, especially when the weather was really bad, began to take a toll after a few days.

In retrospect, I wish I had researched more camping options and committed to reaching those locations.  Knowing that I was going to be some place I could depend on, even if it took a couple extra miles, would have helped me push through.  I think that’s how Michael, and Graeme and Rachel succeeded.  Michael did a lot of wild camping, but he always had a solid idea of where he would stop for the night.

Finding trail markers can be challenging.  Markers can be hidden behind overgrown foliage, barely legible, or missing entirely due to wind and weather.  If multiple trails share the same route, not all the pertinent trails are listed.  Some areas across the moors are completely unmarked, the trail only revealed through the boot prints of earlier walkers.  I used digital maps linked to GPS, a highly-recommended guidebook, and physical ordinance survey maps.  At times, these three sources contradicted each other, and sometimes disagreed with the physical trail markers.

Graeme told me that having a second person to spot the tiny “acorn” markers was a big help.  From my experience, I wandered off trail at least once every day.  Every time I fell, it was because I was trudging across wild terrain trying to find my way back.  I feel fortunate that I wasn’t injured sooner.

The guidebook claimed that there is no reason to bring more than a 12 kilo (26 pound) pack.  I think the book assumes you’re not camping.  My pack was 30.3 pounds without food.  With food, I think I was carrying around 34 pounds.  With the wisdom of hindsight, I would have packed differently.

I wish I had spent the money to buy a lightweight pack in the 45 to 50 liter range, and a lighter sleeping bag, retaining the 20 degree rating.  Together, my pack and sleeping bag came in at nearly 7 pounds, a big chunk of my base weight.

My research indicated that if I packed 5 days of food, it would last me to the end of the trail.  I should have scaled back my packed meals to 2 days.  While accommodations can be hard to find in the villages, food is easier.  The pubs and cafes are frequent enough, and generally close to campgrounds.  “Honesty shops” (little kiosks of food and drink, paid on the honor system) and snack shops are a welcome treat and usually close to the trail.  Hearty snacks like cheese, protein bars and trail mix are good enough when you’ve had either a full breakfast or dinner in a pub.  While the villages don’t have grocery stores, the smaller towns always had at least a convenience store for resupply.

Between a lighter pack and sleeping bag, and less food, I could have easily shaved 5 pounds or more off my total weight.  For me, 27 pounds total weight would be ideal.

Regardless of how gloomy all of the above sounds, I truly enjoyed my time on the Pennine Way.  In fact, I’m already making plans to try again!  I see what went wrong and I’m more confident than ever that the next attempt will be successful.

For more inspiration, I love this video by Fussyphotos.

Round trip airfare from the US cost me around $1,200 about 2 months before departure.  When I was doing my research, that same flight 6 months before departure was around $850.  Book early.

I’ve you’re traveling from the US, an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) is required to enter the UK.  It’s good for one year and cost me about $28.

Train fares from London to Edale, booked 30 days in advance, came to $170.  This required multiple transfers across different transit companies.  If you buy your tickets through an app like the Avanti West Coast, all the required tickets are sold as a bundle.  This app was a lifesaver once I was forced off-trail and had to navigate by train for the remainder of my trip.

Bus and train fares from Kirk Yetholm to Edinburgh came to $40.  Bus routes are managed by each local area, so there aren’t any apps.  However, Google maps was accurate on routes and times and always helped me navigate the bus system.  There is no advance ticket purchase, but I was able to tap a card or digital wallet on every bus I rode.  Even the smallest villages and most remote bus routes accepted electronic payment on the bus.

Pre-booking my hotels 6 months early would have also saved me a lot.  The difference between prices 6 months early and 2 months early was about 40 percent.  Keep in mind that changing exchange rates will affect prices.

A cheap hotel in Manchester and close to the train station, cost me $115 per night.  I went straight from Heathrow Airport to Manchester, avoiding an expensive stay in London.

A major chain hotel in Edinburgh, close to the airport, costs me $255 per night.

On the Pennine, the average price I paid for a double room with a private bathroom was $160 per night. Single rooms with a shared bathroom were often available at 20 to 30 percent less.  Double rooms with only 1 guest were offered at a discount over the same room with 2 guests.  If you’re traveling solo, make sure to adjust your reservation criteria on the inn websites.

Campground fees were generally $13 per night, sometimes discounted for Pennine Way walkers. I’ve since learned that this price can be per person.  I wasn’t aware of this since I was alone.

My original plan was to camp for two nights and sleep indoors every third night.  If I had kept to that plan, I estimate the trip would have cost me about $4,168.  This excludes gear and airfare.  Booking six months in advance would have brought this number down.

My actual costs were quite a bit higher since I spent the second half of my trip off-trail shuttling between various towns and cities.  I had additional transportation costs, and higher average lodging and meal costs for the latter half.

For my next attempt at the Pennine, I’m making several changes:

As challenging as it was, I can’t wait to return and try again.  With a bit of luck and a lot more foreknowledge, I’m going to make it all the way to Scotland!

#8275. Video: The Ultimate Squirrel Rifle

Published Nov 12, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Some people dream of assembling a long-range rifle capable of ringing one-MOA targets at 1,000 yards. Others dream of an ultralight mountain rifle that’s easy to carry for miles and can make a single precision shot. I dream of an ultra-quiet, accurate, and handy rifle for dropping squirrels out of trees. Here’s how I turned a CZ 457 into my dream gun and how it performed in my testing this fall.

The base rifle for this build is a CZ 457 American. I kept the American’s stock because I love a wood stock on a hunting rifle, and its ergonomics work great for squirrel hunting. There are a ton of ultralight chassis you can go with, but wood and squirrel hunting just go together. I did have to sand down the inside of the stock to create room for the new barrel, but that’s easy to do with a palm sander, a dowel wrapped in sandpaper, or every garage gunsmith’s favorite tool: a Dremel.

Lilja makes CZ 457 pre-fit barrels that are fantastic for competition shooting, but I wanted something lighter. That’s why I went with a 16-inch Proof Research pre-fit barrel. One of the great things about the CZ 457 is that the barrel changes are a piece of cake. You simply loosen two set screws to remove the barrel and the new one slides right into the action.

The entire Nightforce NX6 line is fantastic, and the 2-12x F1 variant is perfect for a versatile rimfire. It can take a 50-yard head shot on a squirrel or snap shoot one up close. It also makes this rifle excellent for shooting long range. Dialing in to 300 yards and ringing steel is quite easy with this setup. The scope is fairly light and short, so I don’t think I’m giving up much in terms of weight compared to a traditional 3-9x, but I’m gaining a lot of capability and versatility.

This suppressor is quiet, light, relatively affordable, and easy to clean — everything I look for in a .22 can. There are plenty of other great options like the Dead Air RXD22Ti and the CAT BEN 22 Ti. A .22 silencer is a must-have accessory because it makes shooting a rimfire significantly more fun.

I added an Area 419 CZ 457 Scope Base and bolt handle to my 457 action. The rail makes it much easier to mount scopes and adds some elevation, so I can plink with this rifle out to 300 yards. The bolt handle makes running the bolt easier than the stock round one. One final upgrade I’d like to make is the Timney CZ 457 Trigger.

For accuracy testing, I shot SK Rifle Match, Lapua Center X, and CCI Select. I shot five, five-shot groups with each. All three averaged around a 1/2-inch group at 50 yards. I was most impressed by how well this barrel shot CCI Select, which is relatively inexpensive compared to other ammo I shot.

The new barrel is definitely accurate, and it also made this rifle significantly easier to maneuver in the woods. With the rifle slung over my shoulder it was unobtrusive as I weaved my way through thick cover. When I saw a squirrel, the rifle came to my shoulder quickly and was easy to get stable.

The result of this build is a rifle that’s fun to shoot on the range and a joy to carry in the woods. To me, it perfectly blends a nostalgic wood-stock rifle with modern features. Is it a bit extreme for a squirrel gun? You betcha. But I love this rifle all the same.

#8273. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8271. Saying Goodbye to our Camino Tramily

The next morning, our entire tramily caught a bus from Finisterre back to Santiago de Compostela. Even though the drive was only about 60 miles, the journey took over three hours.

Our bus snaked around the coastal cliffs all the way to the town of Orro before finally heading inland. It felt like we stopped in almost every small town along the Galician coast!

Our driver was incredibly skilled at maneuvering the narrow, winding roads. Every so often, the bus would come to a sudden halt in the middle of the road because the passing lane was barely wide enough for a single vehicle.

Looking out the window, waves crashed far below us. At times, the sheer dropoff to the ocean sat right at the edge of the pavement, guarded only by a short stone wall. Depending on who you asked, the ride was either thrilling or terrifying—but I trusted our driver completely. (A few passengers, however, definitely suffered from carsickness along the way!)

Once we arrived at the bus station in Santiago, it was time to say our final goodbyes to the tramily.

While we knew we would deeply miss their company, everyone felt excited for the next chapter of the journey.

After we exchanged big tramily hugs, the very first thing Knockerz wanted to do was head straight to Burger King for a predictable meal. A lot of our dining on the trail—especially when ordering hamburgers—has been a gamble regarding what kind of meat you actually get!

With lunch out of the way, we kicked off the final leg of our Camino journey by heading south, traveling in the opposite direction of almost every other pilgrim on the trail.

Over the next two weeks, our itinerary includes a mix of several beautiful variants:

Because we don’t have enough time left to walk all the way into Porto, we plan to hike as close as possible. From there, we will take a short bus ride into Porto for a rest day (a “zero”), before flying to Paris and back home to the States.

Heading south took some mental adjustment. Everyone we passed was walking toward Santiago, and all of the yellow shells and arrow blazes were oriented for northern northbound travel.

As a result, we constantly had to check our maps and make course corrections whenever we missed a turn. This leg of the Camino will definitely require constant vigilance.

After climbing out of Santiago along a mix of paved roads, dirt paths, and tight alleyways, we quickly made it to our final destination for the day: Millandoiro.

Millandoiro is a modern, cozy town. Our hotel felt surprisingly upscale while still being very affordable compared to prices back home.

We spent the evening exploring a large grocery store located inside a small local shopping mall. The atmosphere felt familiar—teenagers hanging out away from their parents, and young families strolling through the concourse.

Inside the grocery store, the sheer volume of options overwhelmed us. It made us realize how spoiled we are in the States with massive supermarkets! Ultimately, we picked up prepared meals, drinks, and snacks.

Best of all, the front of the store featured a dedicated kitchen area with tables, microwaves, and utensils—a feature that only a tired hiker can fully appreciate. We happily heated up our dinner, relaxed at a table, and returned to our hotel room to unwind for the night.

#8265. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”

#8264. No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

Published Nov 12, 2026 5:46 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio. The property, which is owned by a family friend, has rolling hills and steep hardwoods and is scattered with hayfields.

“I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan. “I found good deer sign, with lots of buck rubs on trees.”

Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait. Instead, when the season opened, he just walked the woods, scouting and hunting different locations. He used a lightweight tree saddle and climbing sticks to check areas quickly and quietly.

“I sat in six different trees over 12 hunts, moving according to wind and weather conditions,” says the 26-year-old, who works in heavy construction.

On the morning of Nov. 7, he hunted a pinch point where he knew a few does were bedded.

“But I didn’t like the place and started walking the farm again when I climbed down that morning.”

It was the first cold day of autumn, cloudy and with temperatures around 40 degrees. Talbott located a couple of fresh scrapes, and climbed into a nearby tree around 1:30 p.m. to hunt that afternoon. He didn’t see much until about 4:30. That’s when he spotted a big deer headed his way along the field edge.

“I knew he was big, and a shooter, and it all happened very fast.”

When the buck stepped behind some brush 15 yards from Talbott, he drew. The deer stepped into an opening, and Talbott released his arrow.

Talbott saw the deer run about 30 yards and, pouring blood, enter the timber toward a distant hayfield. Then it disappeared over a hill.

“I was shaking uncontrollably when I called my wife, dad, and best friend [Brady Garren] and told them what had happened,” Talbott says. “Dad and Brady got there after sunset to help me look.”

Carrying flashlights, the three men followed a blood trail for about 150 yards. But the trail petered out. Then they heard thrashing in a nearby ravine. Thinking it might be Talbott’s buck, they backed out and called in Triple BC Deer Drone Recovery for assistance.

“They got there with a drone a couple hours later,” says Talbott. “They flew the drone to where we last found blood and in just a minute the buck was found in the ravine, but its head was up.”

They waited an hour and flew the drone again but saw just a slight movement from the buck. An hour later when they flew the drone a third and final time, they saw the buck was dead.

By then, around 11:30 p.m., more friends had arrived and seven people went into the ravine to help haul out Talbott’s huge buck.

“I knew he was a great buck, but I had no idea he was that big until I walked up to him,” Talbott says. “I was beyond ecstatic.”

It was after midnight by the time they field dressed the buck and dragged it 600 yards to the truck. They loaded it and drove to a friend’s cooler.

The next day Talbott’s wife, Alison, took photos before they caped the buck and processed the meat. The buck has 16 points and is an estimated 5.5 years old.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

“My taxidermist says it should score about 190 inches,” says Talbott. “The whole thing is so unreal I can’t explain how I feel. I spent a lot of time there hunting and learning the farm, how to use the wind and where the deer were bedding and scraping … It’s just an incredible experience.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8262. New Bear Canister Requirements on Georgia AT Spur Mass Migration of Bears to North Carolina

CHATTAHOOCHEE-OCONEE NATIONAL FOREST, GA – A recent order by the US Forest Service requiring bear-resistant canisters on the Appalachian Trail in Georgia has caused a dramatic stir in the bear populations local to the area.

According to naturalists, most bears have chosen to “up and leave,” seeking more fruitful prospects in the less-regulated forests of North Carolina. Witnesses have seen hundreds of bears traveling north along the Appalachian Trail corridor, preparing to hibernate closer to what will likely be next spring’s more plentiful food source.

Map of Area Requiring Bear Canisters, via Appalachian Trail Conservancy. https://appalachiantrail.org/news-stories/bear-canister-requirements-georgia/

Human-bear interaction has been on the rise for decades in Georgia due to an increase in overnight hikers, with the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) referring to this inter-species mingling as “conflict” due to hikers “improperly storing food.”

In contrast, delegates of the Georgian bear population describe these interactions as “mutually beneficial” and “charitable.”

“For decades, we bears have benefitted from the abundant gifts generous thru-hikers have left us,” one bear told The PUD. “Every campsite is a bountiful buffet of ramen, Snickers bars, and Mountain House delicacies. The relationship is reciprocal too. Hikers feed us, and in return they get a cool story or sometimes a picture.”

Given that many spring hikers in Georgia are new to backpacking, critters not only feast on poorly placed bear hangs and left-out trash, but often enjoy heartier items more seasoned thru-hikers would consider too heavy to carry, like fresh fruit or packaged meals. For the bears, it has been good eating.

But this cushy lifestyle is now at risk. The official order was signed by the USFS Chattahoochee-Oconee Forest Supervisor in Gainesville on November 6 and will go into effect January 1, 2027. According to the legal document, “All persons camping overnight must possess and use a bear-resistant canister for the storage of all food, food containers, garbage, and toiletries.”

Black bears migrate northbound out of Georgia. Photos by Diego Delso, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Edited with Photoshop.

Following this new policy announcement, hundreds of bears have begun their northern migration to North Carolina, choosing to hibernate closer to next spring’s food source. Wildlife biologists are describing this mass exodus as the greatest bear relocation event since post-glacial habitat shifts across North America and Europe in the late Ice Age.

The exact route to North Carolina can differ for each bear, but many are opting to travel on the Appalachian Trail, given its mostly wooded and well-marked trajectory. Ironically, many bears have imitated the hikers that have caused their migration, creating detailed hike plans with similar mileage to their human counterparts. Sadly for some, the long days of walking have even resulted in a form of Hiker Hunger, which biologists agree is not ideal for a creature that will soon be hibernating.

For most traveling bears, the journey does not end at the Georgia-North Carolina border, as the region already has a healthy bear population. Some Georgia bears have traveled as far as the Nantahala Outdoor Center. Staff at the NOC Outfitters promptly locked their doors and watched safely through the windows as the new arrivals crossed the bridge to scrounge for leftovers at the Big Wesser Riverside Pub.

The new settlers are optimistic that the area will support their growing numbers this coming spring, counting on AT thru-hikers to immediately ditch their bear canisters and forgo any type of bear-proof food storage the second they leave Georgia.

While most bears have joined the trek north, some remain in Georgia, banking on some thru-hikers improperly closing their canisters or simply ignoring the new guidelines altogether.

For those few bears staying, the reality of a changing food source is not overlooked. One holdout remarked that she knows it will be different, but she is willing to give it a try:

“We hope the new backpackers will be carrying so much that they can’t fit it all in their canisters.”

One particularly old bear has been the most vocal about remaining in Georgia. A long-time critic of the US Forest Service and a self-identified “Li-bear-tarian,” the elder Ursid calls the new guidelines “a blatant act of government overreach.”

“I’ve lived here my whole bear life and I’m not going anywhere,” the senior creature told The PUD through graying hackles. “I don’t need those Gainesville statists telling me, or any hiker, for that matter, what we do with our food. This is a free forest, ain’t it?”

As a closing remark, the Li-bear-tarian added, “You don’t live in the backwoods of Georgia if you can’t live the backwoods lifestyle.”

Story by The Pointless Up and Down (PUD) News @PUDThruHikingNews. This article is satire. The events and quotations described are fictional.

#8258. Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb.
