#8165. Best 20 Gauge Shotguns of 2026, According to Our Expert

For a do-everything 20-gauge, the Beretta A400 is the best overall pick, with gas operation and a stock recoil reducer making it the softest-shooting option available. For break-action shooters, the Beretta 686 Silver Pigeon leads the over/under category and the Fabarm Autumn tops the side-by-side. Hunters watching their budget should start with the CZ-USA Drake.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Smallbores are in right now, and 20-gauge shotguns are having another moment. This current trend should last for a long time, too. New ammo for 20-gauges makes them almost as capable as a 12-gauge. As more hunters turn to the 20-gauge as their main gun, gunmakers are offering more choices, including dedicated models for waterfowling, turkey hunting, upland hunting, and clay shooting.

There’s a lot to like about a 20-gauge. Twenties are light and easy to carry. They’re trimmer, too. For some, the lesser bulk of a 20 makes it easier to shoot. The smaller payloads of shotgun shells produce lower recoil so long as the guns aren’t too light. As with all shotgun gauges (except the .410), the 20 gets its name from the number of lead balls of bore diameter that add up to one pound. That equals a bore diameter of .615 inches, which, combined with the 3-inch chambers found on most 20s, means shells can hold up to 1 5/16 ounces of lead or dense TSS shot, 1 ounce of steel, and 1 ⅛  ounces of bismuth. And the 20 can still shoot the mild ⅞-ounce target and dove loads. Here are the best break-action, pump, and semi-auto 20-gauge shotguns you can buy right now.

If you want one 20-gauge gun for all types of wing and clay shooting, the Beretta A400 fits the bill. It combines the already soft recoil of its gas operation with a stock-mounted “Kick-Off” recoil reducer, making it the softest-kicking 20-gauge you can buy. At 6 ¾ pounds, it’s on the heavy side, but not so heavy that it’s hard to carry in the field. And that weight makes it easy to swing and further reduces recoil. The heavier weight combined with a mid-bead, enlarged bolt handle, and bolt closer makes this gun at home at the gun club as well as in the field.

Some shooters with smaller hands struggle with the safety mounted at the front of the trigger guard, and there are better choices for guns that will only be used for upland hunting. But for ducks, doves, and clays, the A400 is ideal, and it would perform just as well in tall grass for pheasant hunting.

Popular just about everywhere, the 686 Silver Pigeon is built around an action that is both very strong and low-profile. The low profile helps the gun point naturally for many people. The ingenious locking system, which consists of conical pins projecting out of the breech that fit into holes on either side, actually sets deeper with use. This is a very hard gun to wear out.

The basic Silver Pigeon has a satin-finished walnut stock and a silver receiver decorated with traditional scroll and grape leaf, with blued barrels. It has a single selective trigger and ejectors, and the stock has a pistol grip and Schnabel forend. At just 6 ¼ pounds, it sits in the sweet spot: light enough to carry, but heavy enough to shoot. Beretta Silver Pigeon safeties are often sticky, but it’s an easy job for a gunsmith to make them work easily.

The Fabarm Autumn is only made in 20 gauge, but that’s okay because the frame is perfect for this light, trim bird gun with classic lines. The Autumn is built on Fabarm’s sturdy four-lug (most side by sides have two) action, originally designed for the rigors of live pigeon shooting. It will hold up throughout your lifetime, your kid’s lifetime, and your grandchildren’s lifetime.

The gun has oil-finished walnut, a case-colored frame, and beautiful, if non-traditional, art-nouveau deep-relief engraving. It has choke tubes and, despite its old-school looks, will shoot modern steel without a problem. A single selective trigger comes standard. Purists have to pay extra for double triggers.

If you want a break-action gun that won’t break the bank, check out the CZ Drake. You can spend less on an O/U, but if you do, you’re getting a cheap 20-gauge shotgun that may give you trouble. CZ guns work reliably, and in those rare times they don’t, they are backed by excellent customer service. You get dependability with the Drake, not the frills. It has plain walnut with a satin finish and black-chrome metal parts for an overall subdued look.

CZ left the mid-rib between the barrels out to lighten them and improve the gun’s balance, which is still a bit barrel-heavy. It has extractors that lift shells for hand removal in place of ejectors that pop them out. You also get 28-inch barrels whether you want them or not; that’s the only choice offered. The Drake is a versatile gun, too, heavy enough for doves, duck loads, and some clays, but not so heavy it’s a burden. The gun does come with five choke tubes and retails for $699. It’s a great value.

Browning revived the classic humpback profile of the original Auto 5 in a brand-new package when it first introduced the 12-gauge, then the 16-gauge A5. While it resembled John Browning’s original Auto 5, the new gun is a completely different design, operating on the inertia principle made famous by Benelli. Besides bad-weather reliability and clean operation, inertia guns are also light and trim, with no gas system parts up front.

The 20-gauge Browning A5 weighs just 5 pounds, 11 ounces, making it a great carrying gun for quail, grouse, and woodcock. With its 3-inch chamber, it can handle heavier magnum pheasant and non-toxic loads. The A5 comes in a glossy walnut version and several camo patterns. Although it does wear Browning’s excellent, effective Inflex recoil pad, it will recoil harder than many 20s because it is so light and because inertia systems don’t reduce recoil as well as gas systems. For the walking bird hunter who wants the firepower of a semi-auto, however, this gun should be ideal.

The Mossberg 500 passed the Test of Time a while ago. Introduced in 1960, it has served admirably as a hunting, home defense, military, and law-enforcement shotgun for 66 years now. The 20-gauge 500 is a lightweight, versatile platform that comes in a basic field model with a hardwood or synthetic stock, as well as dedicated turkey, youth, deer, and even tactical/HD models. The guns don’t have the glossy finish or walnut stocks of your grandfather’s pump, but they are slick out of the box, and they work. They have vent ribs, front and middle beads, and they are drilled and tapped for optics. I made a 20-gauge wood-stocked Bantam model into my 20-gauge turkey gun last year, and it served me well through three states and three turkeys. There’s a 20-gauge 500 for any purpose, including a rifled-barrel deer model. Whatever you choose to use a 20-gauge Model 500 for, it will not fail you.

If you go to a South American dove lodge where the rental guns might fire 1500-2000 rounds a day, chances are good they will be Montefeltros. Benelli’s inertia action is very reliable, and it stays cleaner longer than gas guns, ensuring Montefeltros will keep shooting after other guns fail or even break down. You may not need that level of reliability here, but it’s nice to have it on your side, just in case. Two years ago, Montefeltros received a makeover. They were restyled to look more contemporary. More importantly, they’re easier to load than the old models. The new guns have softer mag and shell-latch springs, and unlike older Montefeltros, they load like butter. Even better, they now use Benelli’s Easy-Locking bolt, which cannot be bumped out of battery and cause a misfire, as can happen with many inertia guns (including older Montefeltros).

The popularity of the 20-gauge means there are lots of twenties on the market to choose from. I stayed away from dedicated turkey, deer, and home defense guns and kept this list more general. All of the guns here are made for wing shooting, and most can go from the dove field to the duck blind to the uplands without missing a beat. I’ve had a chance to shoot these guns, with one exception, and judge them by the following criteria:

These days, you’ll read and hear a lot about how the 20-gauge can do it all and that no one needs a 12-gauge anymore. People said the same thing in the 1950s when the 3-inch 20-gauge magnums first appeared. They were wrong then, and they’re wrong now. In almost any head-to-head comparison, the 12-gauge wins. Period. However, 20s absolutely have their charms and their uses, and you can use a 20 for all your hunting if you choose. You’ll be a bit more limited in range if you do. Or, you can confine a 20 to its real place: the uplands and the dove field, where it excels.

Another factor to consider is weight. Light guns feel great when you pick them up, and they are easy to carry if your hunts take you miles across hard country. Super-light guns are fine for birds that flush in your face or ducks hanging over decoys. Any time you have to swing the gun, however, more weight is your friend, and that goes double on the clays course, where weight not only helps your scores, it saves your shoulder. Think carefully about what you’ll use your 20-gauge for, and choose accordingly. But, definitely pick one. Or more than one. No one should do without a 20.

A pellet from a single shot will fly just as far as the same pellet fired from a single shot at the same velocity from any other gauge. The limiting factor on the 20-gauge’s range is pattern density. As patterns spread downrange, the more pellets in the payload, the longer the pattern remains dense enough to put enough shot on target to make a clean kill or solid break. A 12-gauge, which can shoot heavier payloads, will be more effective at long range.

A 20-gauge shotgun is best for upland and dove shooting. An upland 20 can be lighter than most 12s for easier carrying and still shoot heavy enough loads for any game bird. In the dove field, a 20 has enough reach for most reasonable chances, and recoil will be less, provided the gun isn’t super-light. It is also a great gun for skeet and sporting clays.

The difference between the 12-gauge and the 20-gauge is the bore diameter. A 12 measures .729 inches at the muzzle, while the 20 has a .615-inch diameter. That means the bigger 12-gauge can hold more shot, although there is overlap between the two. A 12-gauge can shoot payloads as light ¾ ounce all the up to 2 ¼ ounces of lead or 1 ½ ounces of steel. The larger bore tends to shoot better patterns as well.

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

Phil Bourjaily sold his very first outdoor story—a feature about snipe hunting—to Field & Stream in 1987. He became the brand’s Midwest regional editor in 1995, and the shotgun columnist shortly thereafter. Highlights Education Bourjaily graduated from the University of Virginia with a major in Art History. He also met his wife, Pamela, at college, so his years in Charlottesville weren’t entirely wasted. Experience Bourjaily has written for numerous shotgunning and wingshooting publications, and appeared on Field & Stream’s Gun Nuts TV show, as well as on DUTV and Clay Target Shootout, which received a Telly Award.He enjoys writing about shotguns and all forms of wing and clay target shooting and has traveled widely to hunt upland birds, waterfowl, doves, and wild turkeys. He also enjoys teaching people to shoot, and has coached scholastic sporting clays and trapshooting. #8164. 2027 Winter Gear Guide: The Best Skis, Boots, and Outerwear of the Season

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

A SKI Test at Deer Valley, a boot test on Mount Hood, and 430 days testing ski pants later, this is the ski gear worth the money. (Photo: Re Wikstrom)

A skier’s fall ritual: taking inventory of the gear closet. What stays, what goes? The jacket survived another season, the boots are fine as long as nobody asks questions, and the goggles might be saved by a new lens. Eventually, something has to be replaced, and everything on the ski shop racks has a marketing pitch. The 2027 Winter Gear Guide is our case for what’s actually worth the money.

Our men’s ski pants testers alone logged 430 ski days last season, which is a lot of time to find out whether a pant seat is truly waterproof. Spread that scrutiny across skis, boots, outerwear, and accessories and you get the 2027 Winter Gear Guide: more than 400 products, a SKI Test at Deer Valley, and a ski boot test on Mount Hood (50 pairs, 10 testers, two weeks).

Of those more than 400 products, 20 earned highest honors. Best in Test is reserved for the winners of SKI Test, our annual ski shootout at Deer Valley, where each ski goes head to head with a full category field and comes out on top. Editors’ Choice goes to gear that brought new tech that changes how well the product works, proved themselves season after season, or surprised us in a category where nobody saw it coming. Best Overall is the simplest: the product that tested better than anything else in its category.

If you’re on the hunt for new gear this season and only the best will do, start here. Each pick links to its full roundup, where you can see how it stacks up against the competition and read the cons—we always have cons.

Few skis have defined a category like the Enforcer. At 99 millimeters underfoot, it’s built for skiers who attack the whole mountain, from refrozen groomers to chopped-up afternoon snow. Its heft keeps it calm where lighter skis get bounced around, and edge grip on firm snow is a standout. The tradeoff is effort: it rewards sharp technique, floats less well than its width suggests, and can feel like work in bumps. Expect a driver’s ski. Read the full review.

Women who spend more time off the groomers than on them will find a willing partner in the M-Pro W 98. At 98 millimeters, it moves between corduroy and off-piste chunder without hesitation, and its stability builds confidence when speed climbs. It’s a directional, big-mountain-leaning ski, which means it asks for strength and a committed stance. Lighter or less aggressive skiers may find it beefy. For rippers who want one ski to charge anywhere, it delivers. Read the full women’s all-mountain ski guide.

The M-Free 108 won Best in Test without winning a single performance category, a reminder that consistency beats flash. Testers found it versatile enough to cover a wide range of terrain, and it floats like a ski much wider than its 108-millimeter waist. That makes it a smart pick for freeride-minded skiers who want one pair for storm days and everything in between, rather than a specialist that shines in only one condition. Read the full review.

Where some wide skis chase fun, the Santa Ana 102 chases speed. It stays calm through chopped-up snow and meets every snow type with energy, as long as the skier can match it. That’s the catch: lesser-skilled skiers may find it unforgiving, it’s stiff in bumps, and driving it takes real leg strength. For strong skiers who want a 102-millimeter ski that rewards commitment and holds its line when the going gets tough, it’s the benchmark. Read the full review.

The Mantra name has long meant power, and the 88 shrinks that formula into a frontside ski. Testers praised how smoothly it rolls from one edge to the other, with a responsiveness closer to a race ski than most frontside designs. It’s stiff and demanding, and the tip can deflect when snow gets cut up, so it’s happiest on groomed and firm terrain. Pick it if you ski fast, ski hard, and want a precise tool. Read the full review.

If you want a frontside ski that takes the guesswork out of starting a turn, the Arcade W 88 is it. A big tip pulls you into an arc intuitively, and it handles groomers, bumps, and mixed snow with equal composure. It wants to stay on edge, so it’s not the choice for sideways, slarvy fun. Skiers who prefer a grippy, predictable ride across changing conditions will find a trustworthy everyday partner here. Read the full review.

Carving skis have drifted wider and friendlier, but the Montero AX still feels like race ski’s cousin. With an 80-millimeter waist, it tips onto edge with little effort and stays planted at speed, rewarding skiers who drive it with intent. The price is steep, and less assertive skiers may find it unforgiving. If you live for corduroy and want a ski you can trust when the speedometer climbs, this is the one. Read the full review.

Powder skis can be lively or powerful, rarely both. The Antimatter 114 manages it. Generous rocker at the tip and tail plus a 114-millimeter waist keep it on top of deep snow, while the ski still feels energetic when you hit it hard. It’s a lot of ski for intermediates and comes only in long lengths, and a few testers noticed some wobble in a straight line at full speed. Expert-leaning powder hounds will love it. Read the full review.

Armada’s Locator 112 is a touring ski with a soft-snow personality. At 1,575 grams per ski, testers found it exceptionally playful in powder. It gives up some reliability on firm snow and isn’t the most nimble in tight terrain, so it’s best matched to big, open lines and storm-day objectives rather than icy couloirs. Choose it when your plan is untracked snow and a lively ride. Read the full review.

A liner refresh, not a redesign, keeps the Shadow MV on top. It suits skiers who equate comfort with a precise, snug fit rather than extra room, with a 100-millimeter last and a progressive flex that transfers power straight to the ski. Testers liked the shin fit and flex feel, and the liner’s design helps avoid pressure points. It runs slightly short, so size carefully. Read the full review.

Tecnica’s Mach 1 is a perennial favorite in SKI’s boot tests, and the women’s TD2 version earns Editors’ Choice by being easier to live with. It’s simpler to get on than past generations, fits a broad range of foot and leg shapes, and delivers a quick, snappy flex that translates to rapid edge response. On fit: Ankle pockets may bite at first. Read the full review.

The Radical Pro is a midweight touring boot that doesn’t feel like a compromise. At 1,400 grams, it offers a remarkably free 60-degree range of motion for climbing, then stiffens progressively as you flex forward for the descent. Fit is generous through a wide last, which suits many feet but may feel cavernous on narrow ones. For backcountry skiers who need one boot to handle long approaches and confident skiing, it makes a strong case. Read the full review.

Raide’s TourTech is a shell built for people who earn their turns. It breathes well when you’re working hard on the skin track, packs down small enough to stash when the sun comes out, and carries thoughtful backcountry touches. The tradeoff of a shell is warmth: on the coldest storm days you’ll need to layer underneath. It isn’t cheap, but for women who tour more than they lap lifts, it earns its Editors’ Choice. Read the full review.

Fit is the whole argument for the Bigline Bib. The cut has plenty of room for puffy long underwear, but three adjustment points (waist cinches, long suspenders, hem buttons) snug it down so nothing drags or sags. A soft three-layer Pertex Shield outer reliably deflected soggy Pacific Northwest storms. Thigh pockets swallow a skin each, so slackcountry laps are covered. These are uninsulated, so be sure to layer up for cold days. Read the full review.

Testers had a hard time finding fault with the Chariot Primo, which is a rarity among women’s ski pants. Its hybrid fit is relaxed enough to layer and move in without getting baggy, and short, regular, and tall inseams let you skip the tailor. Three-layer PNW Primo fabric offers 20,000 millimeters of waterproofing, and TechSteel kick patches guard the cuffs. With no insulation, you’ll need to layer for the weather, but we love these bibs’ versatility. Read the full review

A former Editors’ Choice winner, the Defiant Shell takes the best all-around honor among men’s jackets on comfort, weather protection, and smart details. Venting is excellent, the pocket layout is generous, and the double front zipper is a thoughtful touch. In stormier conditions, its proprietary membrane kept wet, heavy flakes from soaking through. It’s uninsulated, so you control warmth with layers. Read the full review.

Salomon’s Skarn Prime earns the overall nod in the goggles category by doing a lot well. A toric lens gives an expansive field of view, the face foam is layered three deep, and the magnetic lens swap is quick and intuitive. It also pairs with a wide range of helmets. The catches are fit and price: it’s sized large, so smaller faces may swim in it, and $295 is steep. If it fits your face, it’s the one to beat. Read the full review.

Sweet Protection’s Switcher 2Vi MIPS took the overall helmet title on comfort, goggle compatibility, and airflow. The Occigrip turn-dial makes fit adjustments quick, and the 2Vi platform and MIPS layer handle impact protection. Venting is excellent, which helps when the temperature climbs. The only real complaint was bulky ear pads. At 560 grams and $300, it’s not the lightest or cheapest lid, but it covers a lot of ground with few compromises. Read the full review.

Rab’s Guide GTX Gauntlets give you protection without bulk. A Gore-Tex Active shell keeps weather out, 100-gsm PrimaLoft Gold and a high-pile lining supply the warmth, and the low-profile cuff tucks over or under a jacket sleeve cleanly. They’re built to last through a hard season, and Rab also offers an undercuff glove and a mitten version if the gauntlet isn’t your style. At $170, they’re a smart, do-it-all pick. Read the full review.

Swany’s Nexus leans on a new heating platform called ewool and 22-watt-hour batteries, and the result is heat that lasts: up to eight hours on low, four on normal, three on high. Testers liked the haptic feedback when changing settings, the high-quality leather, and that you can charge without pulling the batteries out. A mitt version is also offered for the coldest hands. At $480 it’s an investment, but it’s the heated glove to beat. Read the full review.

#8163. This New Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing)

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

There is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

As the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the new book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

Robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”

Another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

“Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

#8161. The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

This is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other users and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

#8159. Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

But his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”

In September, the artist Iowna Chichowich installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

#8158. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

We did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden said, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling plan was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden said. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”

When things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”

#8157. 17 SKI Editor-Approved Gifts For Hardcore Skiers

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

(Photo: Courtesy of DryGuy, Smith, Peak Performance, Hyperice, The North Face, Skida, Heather Hansman, Black Diamond)

Hardcore skiers can be difficult to shop for.

The more involved you become as a skier, the more specific your wants and needs get. Suddenly, the standard goggles no longer apply, and you choose your jacket not based on what looks cool but on what functions in the ways you need. If you have a dedicated skier in your life, it’s not always obvious what to gift them, especially since you’ll want them to use it and love it.

To help ease your mind, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite gift ideas for the people in our lives who eat, sleep, and breathe skiing: from powderhounds to corduroy snobs, this list has a little something for everyone. And we can guarantee it—we’re somewhat of ski hardos ourselves.

We all have that one friend who complains a little too much about being cold. But when your butt freezes the second you sit on the lift, can you blame them? That’s where insulated knickers come in. Throw them on over your base layers for extra protection your derrière didn’t know it needed. Wear them over your base layer for some extra warmth or on their own for a more loose-fitting base under your ski pants. These are the perfect gift for the skier you know who likes to get a lot of days in and stay nice and toasty on the hill. —Giorgia Menetre, Senior Social Media Strategist

Good goggles don’t need to cost a fortune. Dependable click-in, click-out interchangeable lenses are a staple for a reason—they’ll get you through just about every condition.  Smith’s OG reliable goggles offer a wide field of vision, ChromaPop lenses that make the view pop, and a flexible, comfortable frame. Lenses swap easily, with no worry of a magnetic slip-up. Don’t let another ski day go by letting the skier you love squint through bad light. —GM

These booties come with a high price tag, but they’ll be the gift hardcore skiers never forget. This updated compression boot from Normatec takes the pressurized, full-length boot system that has proven recovery patterns and adds heat. Dynamic air circulation throughout the boot’s treatment session helps muscles recover faster and reduces soreness. Remember how good it feels to put an achy and tired calf next to a hot tub jet? Now, imagine that level of recovery from the comfort of your couch. Boots come in three sizes and can fit a wide range of heights.

Please note that boots will ship the week of 11/23. —Jamie Aranoff, SKI Senior Editor

Hestra’s Fall Line mittens are consistently ranked as some of the warmest by our testers. The mittens have a cozy inner layer of brushed polyester and foam to keep hands insulated without overheating. The outside is leather that, once broken in, is soft and dexterous. Wrist straps ensure that the mittens stay with the skier, and not at the bottom of a chairlift. The mittens are on the pricier side, but will surely be a gift that skiers cherish for years. The same warmth also comes in a glove. —JA

Read our full review and browse other warm gloves and mittens here.

Vests are underrated heroes for skiers: they’re a great midlayer for touring and warmer days, easy to layer, and stylish enough to wear around. The Helium Utility down vest from Peak Performance checks all three of these boxes and more. The vest is incredibly lightweight and packs down into its pocket. More importantly, it’s windproof and water-repellent. A cinch at the bottom allows for customization for the right fit. —JA

If you’ve got an impossible-to-shop-for skier on your list, then look no further: this adventure camera from Nocs Provisions (yes, the same brand that makes binoculars) is sure to please. The camera is incredibly easy to use, even with thick gloves or mittens. Its simple one-button technology allows skiers to easily whip it out of a pocket and hit record (it takes both photos and videos). There’s no SD card needed, and content is easy to transfer to either a phone or computer with cords included. The camera takes retro-style photos and videos and comes with a lifetime “no matter what” policy. —JA

For any serious skier, Dermatone chapstick is the ultimate stocking stuffer. Not only will Dermatone protect lips from chapping, but the SPF keeps skin from burning. It also belongs in every first aid kit; it’s proven to help stop frostbite on extremities like lips, noses, and cheeks. Most ski resorts sell Dermatone somewhere in the shop, but here’s your chance to stock up and avoid inflated prices. Your lips, nose, cheeks, and just about everywhere else will thank you. —JA

Fleeces are always a solid gift, but Ridge Merino’s Alpha Wool Insulated jacket goes the extra mile. This fleece is designed to act as an outer layer for warmer days or uphilling, and a midlayer for when temperatures drop. What makes this fleece different is a mix of strategically placed wool to wick away moisture in places you sweat most, matched with a water-resistant Pertex Quantum Air that acts more like a shell than a fleece.  The fleece is complete with a hood, so no matter the weather, you’ll be prepared.—JA

The North Face just inked a deal with U.S. Ski & Snowboard to outfit the men’s and women’s alpine and freestyle teams for the next eight years. Bonus: They just released a version of the kit for the skiing public. The Comp Team Gore-Tex 2L Freeride and 3L Alpine jackets and pants come in alpine and freestyle designs, but the tech is the same: fully wind- and waterproof with plenty of features such as helmet-compatible hoods,  pit and thigh zips, and a multitude of smartly placed pockets. Don’t forget about the U.S. Ski Team crest on the right chest and all of the relevant sponsor badges to complete the look for your U.S. Ski Team superfan. —Samantha Berman, SKI Executive Editor

Here’s the perfect stocking stuffer for the uphiller on your list—or anyone who wants to add a little flair to their kit. Skida’s Pursuit Headband features the new Alpenbloom print, designed by U.S. Ski Teamer Paula Moltzan as part of the brand’s 2026–’27 collaboration with U.S. Ski & Snowboard. Beyond the athlete-designed pattern, the headband is a genuinely useful piece, made with a moisture-wicking, quick-drying fabric that regulates temperature without trapping too much heat and cozy fleece lining for comfort. A secure, nonslip fit keeps it in place whether you’re skiing, skinning, or working up a sweat on a cold-weather run. For guys, check out Ryan Cochran-Siegle’s Under the Lights print, which comes in a hat and a neckwarmer in addition to a headband.—SB

The Black Diamond Spark Mitts have been a tester favorite for years, and for good reason: you can’t go wrong with a short gauntlet mitt with a full leather outer. But the Spark goes beyond boring old performance. Every few seasons, Black Diamond drops a colorway with a fun, embroidered design on the inner side of the index finger. The Angel Collinson mustache model was our longtime favorite, but the current model with shark teeth is just as fun—and a good reminder that skiing isn’t so serious. —Jenny Wiegand, Outside Associate Gear Director

For the skier who skis in all conditions, this is the midlayer to give. At just 9.8 ounces, the Lightstream Full Zip stays unbulky while delivering serious warmth from -10 to 50 degrees. Vivo Extreme insulation is zoned for the job: 60 grams in the body and collar, 40 in the hood and sleeves, and 25 in the underarms and side seams. The 15-denier stretch nylon/PU ripstop shell is tough enough for daily abuse, and it also works as an outer layer for fall bike commutes and dog walks. Pair it with the Lightstream Insulated Short, made for skiers who run cold but won’t give up their shell pants, even on resort days. Full-length side zips let you take the shorts off when things heat up, without removing your ski pants. Light and packable, they’re also the ultimate emergency layer to stash in your boot bag. Available for men and women. —JW

Carv is the perfect gift for the skier who has everything, mostly because it’s the kind of gadget they’d struggle to justify buying for themselves. But if someone gave it to them? Game on. I’ll admit, I was skeptical of this digital ski coach, which uses sensors attached to your boots to analyze your technique and deliver real-time feedback. But after a few seasons, I’m hooked. It turns improving your skiing into a game, and it’s surprisingly addictive. Ted Ligety once told me his secret to topping the Carv leaderboard: find a stretch of groomer where you can make 10 perfect turns, then ski it over and over until you top the leaderboard. Personally, I might get distracted looking for powder, but I’ve found Carv makes even an ordinary groomer day more interesting. It’s fun, genuinely useful, and exactly the sort of gift someone might not know they wanted. Editor’s note: The list price includes a 12-month membership; continued coaching requires renewal. —Sierra Shafer, Editorial Director, Lifestyle

Few things in skiing are more universally useful than a Voilé Strap. These simple, stretchy polyurethane straps are the duct tape of the ski world, minus the sticky residue. Need to secure your skis together? Voilé Strap. Something breaks on your pack? Voilé Strap. Need to attach something to something else in a way the manufacturer probably didn’t intend? You get the idea. Made in Utah, these little problem-solvers come in a variety of lengths and colors and are practically indestructible. Every skier should have a couple tucked into their pack. Or, if you’re like me, scattered around the garage, the gear room, and the back of the car. You never know when you’ll need one, but trust me, you will. —SS

Why do we organize entire lives around sliding down snowy mountains? It’s a fair question, especially when you consider the expense, questionable career decisions, and occasional sleeping arrangements involved in chasing winter. In Powder Days, journalist Heather Hansman sets out to understand the people who’ve made skiing more than a hobby, exploring the history of ski-bum culture and what happens when the mountain towns that made it possible become increasingly difficult places to live. It’s funny, thoughtful, and at times uncomfortable in the best way, asking big questions about access, affordability, and the future of a sport we love. Give it to the skier who plans their life around winter, or anyone who’s ever seriously considered quitting their job to ski more. —SS

I didn’t win a single race in Alta’s town race series last winter, but I did win this boot dryer in the end-of-season raffle, and frankly, I count that as a victory. Wet ski boots aren’t just smelly. Moisture in your liners compromises insulation, making your feet cold even on mild days and potentially cutting a perfectly good ski day short. And if that moisture freezes overnight? Even worse. This compact dryer uses gentle heat and forced air to dry your boots without damaging their liners. What I love most is that it plugs into both a standard outlet and your car’s 12-volt adapter, so you can start drying your boots on the drive home. It’s also small enough to toss in your ski bag for a trip. Not glamorous, but genuinely one of the most useful things I own. —SS

#8156. Is an AI Data Center Coming for Your Favorite Trail? Check This Map and See

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”

To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.

The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

#8155. Feeling Tension in the Lower-Body After Your Latest Adventure? Do This Simple Stretch.

I often sing the praises of the Warrior I yoga pose (a.k.a. Virabhadrasana I) to skeptical students who feel that it’s a lot of work without a lot of noticeable benefit, so let me explain my enthusiasm for it.

In my work as a physical therapist and yoga teacher, I’ve noticed that many people in our sedentary society have tight hip flexors, which they don’t stretch much, if at all. I’m convinced that short, tight hip flexors are a major factor in many cases of chronic or recurring back pain that so many people experience in the West.

The hip flexors become tight when the hips are constantly placed in a flexed position—think sitting, driving, or sleeping in the fetal position. Like any other muscles, hip flexors will shorten structurally if they are not stretched. However, if you incorporate Virabhadrasana I or Warrior I into your regular practice, you’ll stretch the hip flexors, helping them gradually return to their normal length and easing a source of backaches.

The hip flexor muscles include the iliacus, psoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and, in some situations, the short adductors pectines and adductor brevis. All of these muscles (except the adductors mentioned) cross the front of the hip and are active in hip flexion, which pulls the femur (thighbone) and torso closer together. The hip flexes when you perform a sit-up or lift your leg toward your chest while standing. (Each of these muscles has other actions, too, but we’re focusing here on their hip-flexing ability.)

Of the whole group of muscles, the iliacus and psoas are the strongest hip flexors. They are often referred to as the iliopsoas because they both follow the same path and have exactly the same action. Although they have different origins, the psoas originates on the lumbar spine, while the iliacus originates on the inner surface of the ilium, one of the large bones of the pelvis—they come together in the very back of the lower abdomen and run across the floor of the pelvis, over the outer part of the pubic bones on each side, and dive deep through the inner upper thighs to attach to the inner upper femurs.

The iliopsoas is powerful partly due to its size—each psoas is nearly as big around as your wrist—and partly because its position so close to the hip joint gives it excellent leverage. It is such a strong muscle, in fact, that it can influence the tilt of your pelvis and therefore the position of your spine during your daily activities.

In other words, when the iliopsoas gets very short and tight, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior (forward) tilt. This type of tilt—when the top rim of the pelvis tips forward and down and the coccyx (tailbone) lifts up—usually puts the lumbar spine into hyperextension, also known as a swayback. (A posterior or backward pelvic tilt happens when the top of the pelvis moves backward, the coccyx moves down and tucks under, and the lower back flattens.)

Strong abdominals help pull the pelvis into a posterior tilt, but you might be surprised to hear that even if you have strong abdominals, a tight and strong iliopsoas muscle can win the battle and tilt your pelvis forward.

A chronically hyperextended lumbar spine puts the lower back muscles in a shortened position, causing them to ache. If the only thing that relieves your lower back discomfort is to lie on your back and pull your knees to your chest (therefore flattening the curve), you might have a hyperextended lumbar spine.

Hyperextension also puts a greater percentage of your upper body weight onto the small facet joints on the posterior aspect of the vertebrae instead of on the solid vertebral bodies and disks, where it’s meant to be.

Enter our hero Warrior I, which can stretch the hip flexors, correct an anteriorly tilted pelvis, and help decompress your lower back. But remember to focus on practicing it with a strong posterior pelvic tilt. If you don’t, and your psoas and iliacus are tight, they will pull the lumbar spine into hyperextension, and you’ll eventually feel lower back compression and pain in the pose.

Here’s how to do it. You can also look at this full guide to the Warrior I pose here.

There are several ways to learn how to hold a posterior tilt, but it’s best to learn the action first before integrating it into the pose.

Stand with your back to a wall, with your heels about a foot away from it and your knees slightly bent. Feel an anterior tilt by moving your frontal hip points (the two bony knobs on the front of your pelvis, each known as the ASIS, or the anterior superior iliac spine) down toward your thighs, your coccyx up the wall, and your lower back away from the wall. To move from an anterior to a posterior tilt, lift your ASIS (hip points) up away from your thighs, take your tailbone down the wall, and feel your lower back move onto or toward the wall.

Now that you’re familiar with the action of a posterior tilt, here’s how to incorporate it into your Warrior I.

Set up the pose with your back to a wall, right foot forward, left heel pressing into the wall. Place a strap over the upper thigh in the crease of your right hip and hold it down with one hand on each side of the thigh. Be sure to keep your chest lifted and your shoulders down. If you are in an anterior tilt, your hip points will drop down toward or even onto the belt. To counter that, bend both knees a little and strongly lift your hip points up off the strap and into a posterior tilt. With the hip points lifted, gradually straighten the left knee, pressing the heel into the floor but keeping the lift up on the hip points, in order to stretch the iliopsoas across the front of the left hip.

Keep in mind that for most people, when the front knee bends more deeply, up to the ultimate goal of 90 degrees, it’s hard to hold the posterior tilt. If that’s the case for you, try coming only partway into the pose.

You can deepen the iliopsoas stretch a bit more by minimizing the external rotation of the left hip. When you do this, your left knee will turn out less. The iliopsoas is an external rotator, so it will try to reduce the stretch by externally rotating as you do a posterior tilt.

To lessen this, be sure to turn your left foot 6o degrees away from the wall. (In standing poses like Warrior II, you turn your foot out more, so that it’s parallel to the bottom edge of your mat.) Once you’ve done that, square your pelvis toward the wall across from you as much as you can by pressing the left inner heel down firmly, lifting the left inner knee, and using the strength of the left leg to help bring the left half of the pelvis forward. You’ll not only deepen the iliopsoas stretch, but you’ll also protect your left knee from a twisting injury.

As your iliopsoas stretches and lengthens, it will pull less on your lumbar spine and pelvis, and you’ll be able to lift your lower back up out of the pelvis, thereby decompressing it and relieving discomfort. You may also notice that your posture, both standing and walking, improves, and you might enjoy a new sense of space in your hips and lower back. And you can rest assured that you’re helping prevent arthritis in your lower back.

I hope I’ve made a convincing case for consistently including hip flexor stretches in your home practice. It’s especially important to work them on sedentary days and before practicing backbends—if you’re stuck in an anterior pelvic tilt, you can imagine the compression in the lower back while you do Setu Bandha Sarvangasana (Bridge Pose), Ustrasana (Camel Pose), or Urdhva Dhanurasana (Upward Bow Pose). When you consider adding Warrior I as your iliopsoas stretch, know that you’re setting the stage for a strong and healthy back in the years to come.

#8154. The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

Heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson)

Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

As someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

If you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, New Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

The “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

Norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.
