#8140. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

#8139. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”

Kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most important role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between big and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

As parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8138. What We Learned When Sabastian Sawe Finally Broke the 2-Hour Marathon

In the early 2010s, the idea of breaking two hours in the marathon went from pipe dream to attainable goal. For the first decade of the new millennium, the world’s top distance runners had been chipping away at it. Paul Tergat first breached the 2:05 barrier with his 2:04:55 mark at the 2003 Berlin Marathon. Haile Gebrselassie ran 2:03:59 at the same race in 2008, and by 2014, Dennis Kimmetto held the record with a 2:02:57, less than seven seconds per mile away from sub-two.

Like the four-minute mile, first toppled by Roger Bannister in Oxford, England, in 1954, the two-hour marathon is an enticing target. It’s an even number in a popular event. It’s easy to describe, and therefore easy to market. Perhaps that’s why Nike decided to pour millions of dollars into their Breaking2 project, starting in 2016, bringing Eliud Kipchoge within 30 seconds of the barrier on May 6, 2017, in an exhibition race on the F1 track in Monza, Italy.

After that much-watched effort, Kipchoge became the torchbearer for breaking two hours. His next attempt in 2019 came with a perfectly flat looped course, a roster of pacers blocking the wind, controlled nutrition on a controlled course, and a finishing time of 1:59:40. Kipchoge showed the world that sub-two was possible. He made history. But he didn’t do it in a race.

It would take a special set of circumstances to see the result in a record-eligible setting. An elite athlete would need the right training, the right weather conditions, the right competition. The previous nine times the world record had been set, these circumstances came together in a fall race (Berlin eight times, Chicago once). But at the 2026 London Marathon on April 26, the stage was set. Sabastian Sawe had returned to defend his title, lining up alongside 2025 Chicago Marathon champion Jacob Kiplimo and Yomif Kejelcha, an accomplished track runner making his marathon debut.

On a clear, calm day, the three runners followed pacers through the halfway mark in 60:29. To drop below two hours, they would need to run the second half at least a minute faster, cutting the pace by at least five seconds per mile from their average of 4:37. By mile 18, Kiplimo was falling off the back, leaving just Kejelcha stubbornly hanging on to the shoulder of a hard-charging Sawe. Sawe continued ratcheting the pace down, running the eighth 5K of the race (from approximately mile 21 to 24) in a blistering 13:42—4:25 per mile. But Kejelcha hung on, staying on Sawe’s shoulder until the final four minutes.

When he crossed the line in a time of 1:59:30, Sawe became the first runner to break two hours in a record-eligible marathon. Eleven seconds later, Kejelcha became the second. Kiplimo’s third place time of 2:00:28 was also faster than the previous world record. The two-hour barrier wasn’t broken by an exceptional individual in a one-off performance. Ultimately, a true race with fierce competition and constant pressure was what it took to bring Sawe into the history books.

#8137. Follow This ‘Map of Quietude’ to the Most Silent Trails in Sweden

Taking in one of the many gorgeous views along the quiet Swedish coast (Photo: Andrea Bussell)

The invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden. “The only condition? You have to stay quiet.” Surrounded by apple orchards, with the sea just out the door, this idyllic place would be available to a few lucky travelers—as long as we maintained an air of “quietude” during our respective stays.

Outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health issues: noise pollution. According to the European Commission, prolonged exposure to loud, chronic noise is the second largest cause of health problems contributing to cardiovascular disease, sleep disturbances, and stress-related health concerns. Spending time in naturally quiet environments can help relieve those symptoms.

Skåne is a region renowned for its restorative pastoral and seaside landscapes, unique rural culture, farm-to-table restaurants, and heritage traditions. Within it, The Map of Quietude—a list of 26 places mapped by a professional sound engineer—leads to many spots along Skåne’s 1,000+ miles of hiking trails. Each spot’s silence has been measured to ensure distinctly healing experiences.

I found that pausing in them to take in the stillness and beauty added something beyond a typical travel or hiking experience. It gave me insight into the true frequency of a place and what it offers: peace, an immersion in rejuvenating slowness, and awe. After my days in silence on the coast, I’ve rounded up some best trails where you can easily experience these locations of quietude, while also taking in interesting communities, historic sites, and some of Scandinavia’s most beautiful wildernesses. Sweden’s nature-centric way of life includes the right of public access, or allemansrätten, which allows hiking or camping almost anywhere in the countryside with the expectation that you will respect the land.

Distance: 7.5 miles Part of the Öresund Way, this loop is worth a detour from inland Skåne to discover a car-free island where people come to bike and hike. You can also get some of the region’s best cardamom buns at Hven Durum, a family-run bakery and mill.

A quick ferry will bring you to this tiny slip of seaside heaven. Walk along the coastline and through a species-rich nature reserve for sweeping views of the Öre Sound and Copenhagen skyline. Ven’s southern headland, södra udde, is a nature reserve and designated place of quietude. See an active, mid-20th-century lighthouse nearby. Or, check out the site of 16th-century Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe’s observatory.

Distance: 7.4 Miles (bonus summit extends to 11.4 miles)

Starting at the edge of the Kulla peninsula in northwest Skåne, you’ll trace roughly seven and a half miles of mostly flat shoreline south from the small fishing village Mölle. One of Sweden’s first seaside resorts at the turn of the 19th century, city dwellers came here for their nature fix. Back then, Mölle was steeped in scandal when, after long hikes, men and women began swimming together in the sea nearby, something that was unthinkable at the time.

The route explores nature reserves and gnarled pine forests and winds past beaches and historic towns. You’ll even pass remains of Kulla fälad, a vast historic pasture that served as a shared grazing land for livestock for centuries. In some places, ancient drystone walls are still visible. You’ll end in Höganäs, a globally renowned center of stoneware and ceramics production. It’s also a great place to explore a burgeoning creative community. Stop by The Hub Höganäs to experience local life, where artists sell heritage-steeped crafts, and locals gather for events. If you’re looking for a great place to eat, try Hubben, a local spot run by friendly Swedes.

To visit a place of Quietude, start in the spectacular Kullaberg Nature Reserve. From there, head to Håkull, the region’s highest peak. The summit offers panoramic views of the sea and Danish coastline. It will add about four miles to your trek.

Distance: 117 miles For over 100 miles, the Österlen Way traverses the southeast corner of Skåne. This is Sweden’s famed culinary region. It’s also where my Stay Quiet Cabin was located. Starting in the medieval town of Ystad, the Österlen Way follows the Baltic Sea coast. It passes through nature reserves, national parks, and fishing villages, with inland stretches through ancient forest.

Among other fascinating stops, you’ll pass the hilltop stone circle, Ales Stenar. This is often referred to as “Sweden’s Stonehenge” for its similarly mysterious origins. The trail has two spots of Quietude. The first is Meditationsplatsen, a circular enclosure where people come to meditate. There’s also Gislövshammar Quarry, a 19th-century limestone quarry on the coast of its namesake fishing village. This area is known for its many orchards, farms, and excellent independent shops and bakeries.

Distance: 113 miles This breathtaking route hugs the wave-swept coastline of the Öresund Strait. From north to south, it passes through historic fishing villages and dramatic landscapes. It combines previously mentioned trails and quiet spots (Håkull, Mölle to Höganäs, and Ven Island) with two additional places of Quietude. There are the historic open-air cold bathing houses Pålsjöbaden and Hilleshögs dalar valley.

Hikers pass beaches, meadows, dunes and cliffs, and enter pine forests. The trail varies in difficulty before finishing with a loop around the Falsterbonäset Peninsula. Stone Age graves, medieval castle ruins, and views of the Danish coast keep things interesting. The final legs of the trail provide ample opportunities for birdwatching. It enters nature reserves that are internationally renowned habitats for many of Northern Europe’s migratory birds.

Distance: 994 miles At just under 1,000 miles (1,600 km), the region’s Skåneleden trail is a long-distance route that traverses a vast amount of the countryside’s changeable terrain. You’ll encounter rocky coast, verdant forest, national parks, and nature reserves.  There are also historic sites like castles and stone circles.

The Skåneleden Trail is divided into seven sub-trails by geographic area. There are 148 sections (encompassing all the previously mentioned routes). Many individual sections make for great day hikes. Or, combine them for longer treks over multiple days or weeks. Several sections are near train or bus stations, making transportation easy. Basic campsites with wind shelters and bathrooms are available along the way for those seeking a longer adventure.

**You can hear 60-minute field recordings of birdsong, waves, and wind from each of the places of quietude mentioned above on Visit Skåne’s website or Spotify.

While we don’t always find the best selection of climbing gear at REI, the co-op is currently staging its big Holiday Sale, which lasts through November 23. There are some great steals for climbers in the mix, from a dry rope we love, to a solid shoe pick.

REI doesn’t have all of our top picks in stock, but you may be able to score on some of our favorites this season.

Below are a few of our favorite climbing deals on climbing shoes, ropes, purpose-built pants, and more gear that our editors and testers love.

While not a top pick in our recent shoe guide, we reviewed the Katana Lace in 2024 and called it an excellent shoe for edging and precision placements. It’s also great in narrow cracks and pockets. This is a good first performance shoe for the climber starting to think more about progression, and a great shoe for a climber who cares about performance, but doesn’t want an insanely uncomfortable pair to push their absolute limits. I’ve been climbing in the Katana since last winter and have found it a joy to wear in hand cracks, finger cracks, steep routes, and technical climbs with edging in the gym and on all types of rock. It’s not so great as a comfortable, all-day pair on moderates, or for slab, in my opinion.

Our favorite rope for trad climbing (as of fall 2026), the Black Diamond 9.4mm dry rope balances durability, sleekness, and light weight. During our testing process, we took big whippers, found ourselves hangdogging on steel permadraws, didn’t obsess over the dirt that got into our rope, and ran the 9.4 over grainy lips on sport pitches and across arêtes and edges on mixed and traditional pitches, as well. After months of testing, the rope barely showed any wear, which is notable for a 9.4 that feels skinny in hand and climbs as smooth and airy as an ultra-light—great for rope drag on monster sport climbs or zigzagging trad leads.

At the time of publication, only the 70m was in stock, with low inventory. If you’re climbing in low-moisture areas, you could get the same rope without the dry treatment (also 20% off), or save 20% on the 9.6mm version if you don’t mind the larger diameter (this version is a bit pricier because it’s bipatterned, making it easier to find the middle—worth the premium, in our opinion).

Our best all-around harness of fall 2026, the Black Diamond Solution uses what it calls Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. Our testers loved the contoured hip support and the durability of this harness. “I took hundreds of falls and [the Black Diamond Solution Guide] gets the highest praise I can give a harness, which is that I never even thought about my harness after a fall,” one of our testers said.

Our top all-around men’s climbing pant of 2025, Black Diamond’s Alpine Light Pants feature a mobility-friendly design. We also selected them as our top women’s pick for trad climbing, multi-pitch routes, and alpine lines. While the Alpine Light pants are out of stock or low inventory right now, the Black Diamond Alpine Pants (which are, as you might expect, a bit less lightweight) are currently on sale. We found that this pant model struck an ideal balance between breathability while moving quickly, and moderately protective in light winds and rain showers with its DWR coating.

One of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

#8135. I’ve Used My Backyard Sauna and Cold Plunge for Over a Year. Now They’re on Mega-Sale.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

I’ve spent the past couple of years turning my backyard into an outdoor oasis. Of all the upgrades I’ve made, the two I use and appreciate most are the Plunge Original Cold Plunge Tub and Plunge Standard Sauna.

I use both regularly, whether it’s after a day skiing or biking, a morning workout, or when I need a break from my computer. I suddenly have a lot more friends, too, but I’m sure that’s unrelated.

Plunge’s Black Friday sale is offering up to 30% off cold plunges and 25% off saunas. They’re still a major investment, but if you’ve been considering either one, now is a good time. Here’s my experience owning both and why I recommend them.

I’ve written before about my firm belief that I’m a better person after jumping into an alpine lake. Unfortunately, living in Salt Lake City, where watershed restrictions put many of our nearest alpine lakes off-limits to swimming, I can’t always get my natural cold-water fix when I need it. But I can walk into my backyard.

In the summer, I use the cold plunge for recovery and relief. We hosted a yard sale on one of the hottest days of the year this July, and I spent the afternoon sneaking behind the garage for a quick dip every hour. It was glorious.

Mine stays at a relatively civilized 55 degrees Fahrenheit, although the Pro Chiller can bring the water down to 37 degrees. Five to 10 minutes is plenty for me. Whether I’m recovering after a few hours on my mountain bike or simply need to clear my head, being submerged in cold water forces me to stop thinking about everything else for a few minutes and just breathe. I get out feeling more awake and clear-headed.

There’s some science to back up that feeling, too. As Outside contributor Greg Presto reported in his article on eight common cold-plunging mistakes, studies have found evidence of short-term mood improvements and reduced muscle soreness, though many of the broader health claims remain unproven. Regardless, I feel better after using it, and that’s enough for me.

The model currently on sale has since been updated, but the original-generation tub I’ve used for roughly 18 months has held up well outdoors. It’s roomy and comfortable, and the app lets me adjust temperature, set session times, track progress, and follow Plunge’s guided challenges.

Because the chiller keeps the water consistently cold without requiring bags of ice, the convenience means I actually use it, which is more than I can say for the several yoga mats I’ve purchased over the years. Maintenance has been much easier than I expected, too. The app reminds me when it’s time to treat the water or clean the filter, and both are quick, infrequent tasks that haven’t required much effort on my part.

In the winter, I love alternating between the cold plunge and sauna. In Outside’s guide to the best home saunas, contributor Dean Stattmann named Plunge’s sauna and cold tub bundle the best option for contrast therapy, citing the convenience of controlling both from your phone. I couldn’t agree more.

In the fall, I schedule the sauna to heat up while I’m at my morning ski fitness classes. I come home, climb in, and, if I’m feeling brave, follow it with a cold plunge. It’s the perfect morning ritual before eight hours in front of my computer. Once ski season is here, I’ll be firing it up when I’m leaving the hill so it’s hot by the time I get home.

I chose Plunge’s traditional cedar sauna because it’s compact enough to fit in my side yard, looks good, and smells incredible. It takes some time to heat up, usually about an hour to reach 180 degrees Fahrenheit when it’s 40 degrees outside.

The standard size is advertised to fit up to five people. While I’ve managed to squeeze myself and three girlfriends inside, it’s most comfortable with two people. The fold-up benches are a smart detail if you want more floor space for movement and stretching rather than seating.

One thing worth knowing before you buy: Installation is a project. The sauna requires a dedicated electrical circuit, so factor in that you may need to hire an electrician. You can assemble both products yourself, but I opted for professional assembly, which you can arrange when you order.

Once it’s up and running, it’s hard to beat having your own personal wellness center a few steps from your back door, especially before or after a day outside. Neither product is a casual purchase, but both are well worth it to me.

#8134. Continental Divide Trail Southern Terminus Monument to Be Relocated Due to Border Wall

A section of steel wall along the U.S.—Mexico border (Photo: PATRICK T. FALLON / Contributor via Getty)

Hikers can once again access the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail, more than two weeks after border wall construction closed down the southernmost 1.1 miles of the trail, the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) says. But with the official end of the route now trapped between two sections of steel barrier, the obelisk that marks the terminus will need to be moved.

The southern mile of the trail had been closed since late October, when crews began widening the road that runs along the border fence and installing a second length of wall. Since 2025, that stretch has fallen inside the Fort Huachuca New Mexico National Defense Area, created when the Trump administration transferred 110,000 acres administered by the Bureau of Land Management to military control.

On Friday, the CDTC said it had received confirmation that hikers would once again be able to access the terminus. As before the closure, anyone entering the NDA needs to apply online for a permit from Fort Huachuca and undergo a background check; additionally, hikers who aren’t U.S. citizens need to be chaperoned by a permitted hiker who is.

“This closure came at a critical time for southbound hikers,” the CDTC said in a statement. “Completing the 3,100-mile trail is a monumental achievement, and the construction activities at the border created dynamic changes to the permitted NDA access in place during the past year.”

However, the construction has created a new issue: The Crazy Cook monument—the stone obelisk that marks the official end of the Continental Divide—is now sandwiched between the two steel barriers that make up the under-construction border wall. In an email, Audra Labert, the CDTC’s director of communications, said that while the organization had received reports that hikers had still been able to reach the monument by passing through the construction area, that arrangement is likely temporary.

“Authorities are now confirming plans to move the obelisk outside of the barrier walls for hikers to access, and passages between the barriers will eventually close,” Labert wrote. While it’s not clear when that could happen, the CDTC warned that the government would likely close the terminus to hikers again while it relocated the monument.

Construction on the border wall has complicated thru-hikers’ ability to access the southern termini of several long trails over the past year. In addition to the CDT, the federal government permanently closed access to the Arizona Trail’s southern terminus last November, a move that Matthew Nelson, the executive director of the Arizona Trail Association told Backpacker was “nothing less than a desecration.” In addition, authorities briefly banned Pacific Crest Trail hikers from touching the border wall this spring before abruptly reversing course. The under-construction barrier continues to figure in access and conservation fights along the southern border, with the Supreme Court recently ruling that the administration could continue construction of a new stretch of wall in Big Bend National Park.

The holiday season is meant to be a time to relax, be with friends and family, and, ideally, get some climbing in. Don’t let the obligation of holiday shopping take up too much of your time—the editors at Climbing have determined what we believe are the best gifts for the climber in your life, whether a gym, sport, trad, or ice climber, a burgeoning mountaineer, an all-arounder, or someone who hasn’t tried climbing yet, but is eager to get started.

Whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh new set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

Ocun’s new Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

Last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

Edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one

The Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a new, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

The Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional big-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

Apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

Black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

Climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

What gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? By donating to Access Fund you become a member of the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, who tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens new ones.

#8130. Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.

Christina making coffee while camping at Big Bend (Photo: Abigail Wise)

“WE ARE VERY close to being able to see Carroll Crater!” Christina Koch shouts across the campground, glancing up from her moonscope.

The NASA astronaut is bent over a small tube that looks like a telescope, attached to a tripod. A nearly full moon illuminates her curly hair, with her tent and a field of scraggly creosote bush behind her. The Big Bend National Park campsite is large enough to sleep eight people, but it’s just the two of us here tonight. Even at 10 P.M., the temperature hovers in the mid-70s. It’s already past my bedtime, but Koch and I came to the park to witness what happens in the sky after dark.

“If you look to the lower left, there’s a dark spot, almost like a mole. Carroll Crater is a little up to the left of that,” Koch says as I bend down to look through the lens, the dark splotches of the moon suddenly massive and detailed to my right eye.

Koch and the other three astronauts on the 2026 Artemis II mission named Carroll Crater after colleague and mission commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife. Mission specialist Koch, Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen made history in April 2026 when they completed a ten-day-long mission around the moon, traveling a record-setting 252,757 miles from Earth, livestreaming the event, and going viral along the way. It made Koch the first woman to travel around the moon, adding another record to her list, which also includes the longest spaceflight by a woman (328 days throughout 2019 and 2020), and embarking on the first all-women spacewalk on October 18, 2019.

FIVE MONTHS AFTER the Artemis II crew touched down in the Pacific Ocean, Koch and I met in Big Bend to go on our own small mission: nighttime photography. Last night, September 26, was a full moon, and it still looks massive, bright, and round above the Chihuahuan Desert tonight. The only way you can tell it’s no longer full, Koch tells me, is that you can spot a little bit of the Terminator in the upper right corner. The Terminator, the line that divides the side of the moon that’s glowing from the one going into shadow, looks like a sliver of darkness that shifts the moon’s craters into 3D.

“Imagine seeing that when it’s literally this big in your view,” Koch says, holding her hands wide.

We’ve spent the evening on a couple-mile hike and scramble up to Balanced Rock to photograph the stars and moon. Balanced Rock is a massive boulder suspended between stacks of rocks on either side so that it appears to hover above the ground. Sitting next to the boulders, Koch set up her tripod and snapped shots of the massive, orange moon rising and the stars sparkling above the syenite rock formations. She even managed to capture the shooting star we both spotted streaking above.

Photography is her hobby, she tells me. She’s been taking pictures since she did so for her college paper at North Carolina State University, from which she holds multiple degrees in physics and electrical engineering.

Her love of photography came in handy for her space missions. NASA, which features an entire photography training team, worked with Koch and the rest of the Artemis II crew ahead of their historic trip to optimize documenting photos of the moon and Earth from space. They had to learn how to use a wide lens as the Artemis II crew occupied a very small vehicle, how to use the proper f-stop and shutter speeds, and how to take more technical photography, too, to report back on anything that appeared broken and other details for the on-the-ground engineers.

Photography wasn’t the only arts-based training the Artemis II crew took on prior to their mission. The four astronauts decided to seek out and collaborate with a poet to assist them in better describing what they saw in space. Koch still trains with the poet today. “He helps me a lot with metaphors and language, but also just seeing the beauty in things,” she says.

The crew’s holistic approach is, in many ways, different from how older generations of astronauts prepared for space travel. The Apollo Generation, which included astronauts like Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, who became the first people to walk on the moon in 1969, focused on thousands of hours of moonwalk and lunar surface simulations and reduced gravity training. While practical, technical skills were vital to the Artemis II astronauts, too, they also concentrated heavily on team dynamics: the crew embarked on a National Outdoor Leadership School (NOLS) trip together, a common practice today for NASA teams. “We made so many commitments to being a crew that loved and trusted each other,” says Koch. “NOLS was one of the things that we did when we learned a lot of those actual skills to keep us in a good place and keep us friends.”

Another focal point for the Artemis II crew was learning about the meaning behind their destination. “We worked with cultural experts on the moon and tried to cultivate a deeper understanding of the many facets of where we were going, not just the scientific ones,” says Koch.

But for the differences in training approaches and communication styles throughout history, the narrative around space exploration has, in many ways, remained the same. “Beautiful concepts like love and peace, and going for all of humanity, those have always been a part of it,” says Koch. “There is almost no one who went [to space] and didn’t have beautiful things to say.”

AFTER A COUPLE of hours taking pictures near Balanced Rock, Koch and I are back at camp, eating dinner under the moonlight. She’s cooked up some simple couscous on a backpacking stove and finishes it with a handful of pine nuts.

“This is how low-key I am,” says Koch, gesturing to her pot. “It’s practically plain couscous, and I’m so excited for it because I was such a dirtbag backpacker for so long. This is very standard and kind of nostalgic.”

Over the years, Koch, who’s 47 years old, has developed an arsenal of dirtbag and outdoors skills. She’s an accomplished climber—mostly sport, trad, and ice—and skis both downhill and cross-country. Despite growing up near the ocean in North Carolina, where her dad taught Koch and her four siblings how to sail, she didn’t begin surfing until her mid-thirties; now it’s one of her favorite sports. She also loves trail running, but after struggling with hip dysplasia for years (the trip to Big Bend was a few months after she had a hip replacement), Koch took up triathlons instead to balance out the running with cycling and swimming. In order to do so, she had to learn to swim distances, which she tackled in her mid-forties. “It took me like two years to learn to swim. I’m very uncoordinated,” Koch insists.

One of Koch’s biggest adventures, outside of the Artemis II mission, took place in 2006 when she and some friends climbed Mount Kenya. The group ascended the 17,058-foot mountain, which requires technical climbing to reach the highest summits, without a porter. The first night camping on the trip, Koch opened the door of her tent after hearing a strange noise; a sea of glowing eyes reflected back at her as a herd of wild buffalo passed by. “I was like, ‘We’re going to get trampled and die,’” she says.

Luckily, the herd moved on without incident, but Koch had another problem: she quickly realized that she hadn’t packed enough food for the ascent. That same night, a ranger came by and had cut his finger very badly but didn’t have a way to sew up his wound. Koch and her friends had a first-aid kit on hand and helped patch up his injury in exchange for a can of beans.

The beans, along with the food she did pack, helped fuel her through the week-long backpacking trip, in which she and her friends carried a lot of weight, hauling their climbing gear up to the technical section of the mountain. While they didn’t make it all the way to the summit they were targeting, they did climb for a stretch of it. “We made it higher than you could walk up,” says Koch.

Coming off the mountain, though, the climbers were out of food and cash, and rather than hike another eight miles, they managed to scrounge together their very last coins to ride a bus back to town. “I must have lost so much weight,” she says. “My pants were hanging off of me, and we were very hungry.”

But they arrived at their target hotel safely and used their credit cards to book a room. “I will never forget the next morning we were eating at an all-you-can-eat breakfast buffet,” says Koch. “It was the funniest dichotomy of going from really feeling like we were at the end of our line, coasting out on fumes, to being completely OK and in the borderline lap of luxury. It was just so ridiculous.”

Professionally, Koch spent several years of her early career traveling to remote, isolated landscapes, conducting scientific research. She always wanted to be an astronaut, but wasn’t interested in pursuing the typical paths astronauts often follow, such as obtaining a degree in aerospace engineering or getting a pilot’s license. “I want to be in nature, not flying over it, so that was just never a hobby that really called my name,” she says.

So while Koch has dreamed of being an astronaut since she was a child, she wasn’t going to give up her interests to pursue some kind of checklist to become one. Instead, she followed her passions for science and nature into often harsh environments. She worked as a research associate for Raytheon Polar Services, stationed in Antarctica, where the area closes down for months at a time due to extreme cold and darkness. “There’s no mail, no fresh food, no people in or out for eight months,” Koch says. “That was something I went and did when I was 25.”

She also worked as an electronics and instrument technician in Greenland, Alaska, and again in Antarctica before traveling to American Samoa in 2012 as a station chief for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). It was there, while stationed in American Samoa, that she met her husband, Bob Koch, who at the time was working as a GIS coordinator.

During a time before smartphones and internet access were a given, Bob quickly figured out that Koch drove by a favorite surf break of his 45 minutes east of where he lived on her way to work each morning. So Bob asked Koch to take a photo of the surf on her commute, and then send it to him over the reliable internet at her laboratory. “She was my surf report buddy, and then obviously things took off from there,“ says Bob, who now works for the Army Corps of Engineers. “We called it Peter Pan Island.”

Not long after meeting, Koch decided to apply to become an astronaut, and when she was accepted in 2013, she and Bob moved to Houston, Texas, where NASA’s Johnson Space Center is based and where the couple now lives with their dog, Sadie. “Going from a full-on dirtbag lifestyle to the most regimented, military-like astronaut training, with these requirements and proficiencies, was like whiplash for me,” says Koch, who used to view more conventional career paths as selling out or growing up. “Everything I did was towards free time and the outdoors and very minimal requirements in life.”

But her thinking soon shifted as she embraced her new job. “I used to think that all of these people working really hard don’t know what life is really about,” she says. “And then I realized, actually, maybe it’s totally OK to work really hard for something and make a difference.”

WHEN ARTEMIS II launched into space from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, the four crewmembers had prepared themselves, each other, and their loved ones for the risks and reality of the adventure they were undertaking. In preparation, the Kochs bought a Sprinter van.

“[Bob] was trying to figure out what do you do when your wife goes to the moon?” says Koch. “You can’t go to work; you’re not going to be able to concentrate. If you’re sitting at home, you’re going to be worried. So he organized a road trip with his friends.”

Bob devised a plan: Mission Break 80, in which he and his friends would golf and surf their way from Florida, where Artemis II launched, to San Diego, where the crew was set to land. They’d camp along the way in his new van, which proudly displayed an Artemis II magnet. As a joke, Bob created Mission Break 80 patches to match. And while he only made it as far as Houston in the van, the distraction largely worked.

“Going surfing every morning took me away from my phone for two hours, or the act of setting up camp and being outside just created a calming effect,” says Bob. “That was my way of coping with the mission: actually spending time outdoors, away from devices, but just close enough in case I needed to get a call.”

Bob got two half-hour calls with Koch during the mission, one on day three and the next on day seven. He took the first call from the beach with wet hair and waves in the background.

One thing the crew and their families had not prepared for was how many people would watch the Artemis II mission worldwide. “Moon joy,” the excitement of the 2026 orbit, as it was dubbed, went viral. NASA reported more than 149.4 million views of the launch, splashdown, and lunar flyby on its own platforms alone. An estimated 400,000 people gathered in person to watch the launch in Florida, according to Smithsonian Magazine. “They kind of caught lightning in a bottle,” says Bob. “I think it was a combination of the synergy of the crew collectively and all their unique personalities and kind of how they played off each other. And I think it was just some timing where people really wanted a positive story that they could follow and all rally around.”

While #moonjoy was trending on every social platform, Koch and the rest of the Artemis II crew were oblivious to the buzz on the ground. “We never dreamed it would become what it was,” says Koch. “We actually might never know what happened on Earth while we were gone,” she continues. “Earth had a party for us, and we weren’t there.”

On the second of their two allotted calls, Bob realized he had to let Koch know how popular the mission had become. He told his wife that she and her colleagues were inspiring people down on Earth. “I told her how proud I was and how inspirational she and the crew and mission were,” he says. “I remember she teared up.”

Koch remembers the call vividly, too. “He was like, ‘Tina, I need to tell you something. Something is happening down here. You guys are having an impact. You’re moving the needle,’” she recalls.

“It’s funny because when you cry in space, your tears well up in your eyes, and they just stay there,” says Koch, explaining that the lack of gravity makes it so that tears don’t fall. “I was wiping my buoyant tears, and I was like, ‘That’s all we ever wanted…’ When we designed our mission patch, it was ‘A II;’ we made it look like the word ‘all.’ That was our goal: for all.”

IT’S NEARLY NOON and the sun is blazing in Balmorhea, Texas. Koch and I just met up to cool off in the world’s largest spring-fed swimming pool, a 1.3-acre body of brisk water in the high desert of West Texas. We’re taking a dip with the locals—kids splashing and shrieking with delight, groups of women floating on inner tubes, and a handful of scuba divers—before driving out into the 91-degree desert to hike and camp.

As we chat and tread water, I glance down to see schools of fish darting around our legs. “Sometimes they bite,” Koch told me earlier, “which is kind of fun!”

If I look long enough, with a little luck, I might even see a turtle, one frequent swimmer mentioned when I arrived. Koch says she spotted them last time she was here on a van trip.

“I’m going to go do some laps and look for turtles,” she tells me, snapping on her goggles and doing the breaststroke over toward the deep end, which reaches 25 feet.

I follow her, trailing behind, gazing into the sparkling, royal blue water. Behind me, a group of teens is taking turns launching off a diving board, and a small family is gearing up to scuba dive. We’ll need to head out soon if we want to snag a camping permit before the park’s visitor center closes. Koch knows it’s time to get going, too.

“I’m just going to jump off of the high dive one time before we go,” she announces, making her way to the opposite side of the pool. As I watch, she climbs out and walks briskly to the edge. She hesitates briefly as she eyes the water below. Then, she jumps, suspended in space for just a moment before she splashes back down to Earth.

Abigail Wise is the brand director at Outside. She’s been fascinated with space since her mom sent her to a science space camp one summer in elementary school. These days, she’s been known to drag her own kids out to watch meteor showers in the middle of December near their home in northern New Mexico—and insists it’s worth every whine.

This article is from the Winter 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

#8129. Rodents Keep Destroying Your Hiking Gear? Here’s How to Keep It Safe

A chipmunk chews its way into a hiker's backpack. (Photo: Stanislav Sablin/Getty Images)

One of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents. I love watching squirrels chase each other around tree trunks, and I may or may not have had a “pet” chipmunk in one of my cabins during a horseback guiding season. I talk to marmots when I’m alone, and hearing the chirp of a pika makes my day. But I draw the line at the little buggers crawling over my face in a shelter, chewing through my trekking pole straps, or getting into my food bag.

This is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite. While no one I know has a perfect mouse-proofing strategy, here are a few tips and tricks to help keep rodents at bay and protect your pack pockets, straps, and food.

The most vulnerable parts of your gear are the deliciously salty pack straps, trekking pole straps, and pockets where you’ve forgotten you left food. While keeping your straps clean is easier said than done after days of sweaty hiking, reducing the tantalizing salty odors will work wonders in keeping sodium-fiending rodents away. If you can, dunk your straps in running water a few times throughout the day, and especially at night when you get to camp.

You can also drip a few drops of hand sanitizer onto trekking pole straps to make them less appealing, and tucking a dryer sheet into salty pockets or around hammock straps can also work as a rodent deterrent. Finally, always stash your trekking poles upright in the ground to keep the straps less accessible.

The bear hang is a time-honored backcountry art form, but if you’ve ever seen an acrobatic mouse shimmy down the rope and land a perfect 10 on your backpack, you know this protective measure doesn’t translate perfectly to rodent-proofing. The solution, as many of us have seen in high-traffic trail shelters, is something I call the Mouse Swing. This is simply your standard piece of paracord or bear-hang rope, but with a barrier tied in the middle.

I’ve used everything from a (clean!!) tuna can to a quart-size yogurt container lid. Punch a hole in the can or plastic lid, run your string through the hole with knots to secure it in place, and you’ll have a lightweight, highly functional barrier between your pack and the string. Make sure your bag is a few feet above the ground or shelter floor to prevent high jumpers from making the leap.

Along with salty straps, mice, rats, and squirrels are highly attracted to food smells. The worst pocket destruction I encountered was when I carefully hung my pack from the rafters of a shelter but forgot to remove the remains of an energy bar from the pocket, and an industrious mouse chewed right through the material. Don’t forget to check your pockets for lip balm, energy gels, or the remains of your lunchtime protein bar.

While a hard-sided bear canister is the best protection against animals getting into your food supply, I prefer not to carry the bulky, heavy contraption unless it’s required in the area. The next best thing is the Ursack Allmitey, a heavy-duty food bag made from Spectra, a specialized material with one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios out there. Once tied properly closed, it’s next to impossible for critters to chew through or squeeze through the opening. If you’re in an area where rodents are the only concern, you can size down in bulk to the Ursack Minor, a Kevlar bag that isn’t tough enough to stand up to bears, but can keep smaller toothy critters at bay.

I’ve also used RatSacks for food drops in the desert. They’re heavier than the Ursack Minor, but have proven virtually indestructible against desert rodents, and some national parks like Canyonlands lend them out for free. These are made from stainless steel mesh with a heavy-duty Velcro closure at the top, and while they aren’t bearproof, I’ve never had a smaller animal bust through the dense metal mesh.

Finally, if scent control is your primary priority, you can further streamline your gear with LokSak OPSAK bags. These won’t prevent sharp little teeth from chewing through them, but the polyethylene material and secure zip tops are completely odorproof and can keep curious squirrels and chipmunks from testing them in the first place.

I hesitate to write this since it’s such a Big If, but if you’re camping somewhere that the risk of running into a bear is zero, you can bring smelly items into your tent. This isn’t foolproof—you run a risk of an unusually bold mouse chewing into your tent—but by and large, most small rodents will be deterred by your massive sleeping form and won’t bother trying to break in.

#8128. Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing new climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

“She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”

Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

“With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” said Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”

Pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”

Pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

#8120. How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest

On May 29, a Nepali high-altitude worker named Hillary Dawa Sherpa ran out of oxygen while descending Mount Everest at the edge of the Death Zone. Days went by, and officials assumed he was dead. And then, six days after vanishing, he crawled on his hands and knees out of the Khumbu Icefall toward Base Camp, where he was rescued by camp workers.

Hillary Dawa’s improbable story of survival ignited a debate about safety and ethics on the world’s highest peak. And the 57-year-old wasn’t supposed to have been on Everest’s highest slopes in the first place.

He was originally hired to work as a seasonal cook at the Camp II setup of low-cost Nepali guiding company Himalayan Traverse Adventures. The company had just two paying clients for the 2026 season: Chris Thrall, a British ex-Royal Marine, and Mariusz Chmielewski, a plumber from Poland.

But late in the expedition, Hillary Dawa was asked to guide Thrall up the mountain, after Himalayan Traverse Adventures sent one of its experienced climbing Sherpas home.

“I was only supposed to be a cook, but they offered me 10,000 Rupees a day to climb with the clients,” Hillary Dawa told Outside. “I didn’t even want to go to Everest this year.”

Outside reached out to Himalayan Traverse Adventures but did not receive answers for this story. Hillary Dawa said company management believed Thrall was incapable of making it above Camp IV. But Thrall eventually reached the summit. Hillary Dawa and Chmielewski turned back before the top and retreated to Camp IV. On the descent, the company’s other climbing Sherpa sped ahead down the peak, while Thrall, Chmielewski, and Hillary Dawa continued together. They were racing toward the May 29 closing date, which is when Sherpas would remove ladder bridges from the Khumbu Icefall.

“I was carrying eight empty oxygen tanks and the client’s sleeping bag,” Hillary Dawa said. “If I lost an oxygen bottle, they would deduct $250 from my salary, so I had to bring it all down.”

Eventually, he ran out of oxygen and sat down to rest, telling Thrall to continue. Thrall and Chmielewski reached Camp II at 23,000 feet and radioed for help, saying Hillary Dawa was in trouble. But Himalayan Traverse did not mount an immediate search and rescue mission.

Days went by with no sign of him. A larger company, 8K Expeditions, eventually launched a rescue. Assuming nobody could survive that long without food and water, reporters increased the season’s fatality rate to six. His family prepared funeral rites at a monastery in Kathmandu.

Meanwhile, high on the mountain, Hillary Dawa fought to live. After regaining consciousness, he inched down, stopping at abandoned tents to search for scraps of food and water. At the Khumbu Icefall, he found safety ropes buried under snow and ladder bridges intact. He was within sight of Base Camp when another disaster struck—a ladder bridge collapsed, sending him plunging 50 feet into a crevasse. He caught a safety rope, which saved his life.

“I looked down and saw a small ledge of snow,” he said. “I kept my head straight and slid down the rope and landed on the ledge. And that’s when my leg broke.”

Injured but alive, Hillary Dawa spent the next two and a half days on the precipice. He survived by eating a few pieces of candy and a packet of instant coffee, rationing the calories carefully and sucking on ice to moisten his mouth. On the night of June 3, his fifth day alone on Everest, an avalanche rumbled into the crevasse. Hillary Dawa braced for the worst.

“I thought about God,” he said. “I prayed: ‘Either let me die here or help me get out.’”

He lived. And in the morning, he saw that the slide had created a snow ramp to the surface. Using his good leg, Hillary Dawa pushed himself backward to the surface. Severely dehydrated and weak, he spent the next day and night crawling through the labyrinth of ice, eventually emerging near Base Camp. Within a few hours, Hillary Dawa became a global sensation.

While his ability to survive against seemingly impossible odds is the stuff of legend, his ordeal also raises uncomfortable questions about who bears the greatest risks on Everest, and what happens when expeditions cut corners.
